Issue Reading note
The fuel shock makes FY2025 stale United paid $2.44 a gallon in FY2025 and $4.19 in Q2-2026, up 71.7%. Every FY2025 unit-revenue, unit-cost and margin figure has been overtaken. Where a full-year figure appears below, the Q2-2026 figure appears beside it.
One operating segment United reports a single segment with net income as the measure, so no segment profit exists. Every business-unit split below is rebuilt from income-statement revenue lines and the revenue note, and the mainline/regional passenger split was withdrawn after the FY2018 10-K.
Two definitional breaks in the leverage series Adjusted EBITDAR was redefined on 1 January 2025 to add back the fixed portion of all operating lease expense, which raised FY2024 adjusted EBITDAR by $662m and moved reported net leverage for 31 December 2024 from 2.4x to 2.2x. ASC 606 (2018) and ASC 842 (2019) recast FY2016-FY2018 revenue, operating income, capex and the balance sheet.
The unit-cost metric management guides to is not in the filings The FY2025 10-K prints CASM but no CASM-ex reconciliation. FY2023-FY2025 CASM-ex exists only in the quarterly earnings releases, so the ten-year series cannot be built from filings alone.
  • The newest company document available is the Q2-2026 8-K of 15 July 2026. Ten weeks of Q3-2026 had elapsed by 11 September 2026, and the global average jet fuel price reached $171.01 a barrel in the first week of September, about $4.07 a gallon before taxes and into-plane cost, against the $3.69 assumption inside the Q3 guide (IATA fuel monitor, accessed 2026-09-11) [web].
  • No sell-side research covering United appears in the subscribed report set (0 of 376 reports), so the external view is built from Bloomberg consensus and recommendation data, from analysts' own questions on the calls, and from dated press summaries tagged [web].
  • Consensus figures are Bloomberg BEst as of 11 September 2026 throughout.

1. Business description, model and unit economics

United discloses ancillary fees only as an annual total and does not decompose them by type. Fees were $4,800m in FY2025, 9.0% of passenger revenue and $26.51 a passenger against $14.77 in 2019, so about a quarter of the per-passenger revenue gain since 2019 came from fees, which the driver tree below cannot separate from premium mix and cost pass-through (10-K FY2025 and FY2019, Note 2).▪

United sells three things: seat-miles on its own and contracted regional aircraft, belly cargo space on the same flights, and MileagePlus miles to JPMorgan Chase and about 110 other partners.▪

Revenue line FY2025 % of total FY2024 FY2023 YoY FY24 YoY FY25
Passenger 53,438 90.5% 51,829 49,046 +6% +3%
Cargo 1,779 3.0% 1,743 1,495 +17% +2%
Other operating 3,853 6.5% 3,491 3,176 +10% +10%
Total operating revenue 59,070 100% 57,063 53,717 +6% +4%

(10-K FY2025, Item 7.)

The revenue equation. Passenger revenue equals capacity times unit revenue: 330,284m available seat miles at 16.18 cents of PRASM gives $53,440m against the $53,438m reported. The same figure reconciles two other ways, 271,619m revenue passenger miles at a 19.67-cent yield and 181,053 thousand passengers at an average fare of $295.15, with an 82.2% load factor linking the first two (10-K FY2025, Item 7 operating statistics). Total revenue equals 330,284m ASMs at 17.88 cents of TRASM.

Passenger revenue component FY2025 $m $ per passenger % of passenger revenue
Ancillary fees (bags, seats, inflight, ticket fees) 4,800 26.51 9.0%
MileagePlus award travel recognised 3,414 18.86 6.4%
Cash base fare (residual) 45,224 249.78 84.6%
Passenger revenue 53,438 295.15 100%

(10-K FY2025, Note 2; passengers from the operating statistics table.) Fees per passenger rose 79% between 2019 and 2025 while the average fare rose 21%.

What an award seat is worth. 10.9m MileagePlus flight awards were used in 2025 and represented about 10.3% of revenue passenger miles, which is 27,977m award RPMs against $3,414m of travel redemptions: 12.20 cents an award RPM against the 19.67-cent system yield, or $313 an award (10-K FY2025, Item 1 Loyalty Program and Note 2). An award seat is booked at 62% of what a paid seat over the same distance produces, and because the redemption line also covers upgrades and partner-airline redemptions while the mile count covers free flights only, 12.20 cents is a maximum.▪

Cargo and mile sales are produced on capacity the passenger business already pays for: a belly-hold ton-mile needs no extra flight and a mile sold to Chase needs no flight at all. On this allocation every dollar of FY2025 operating income came from those two lines while the flying ran $918m short of its fully-allocated cost, against a $667m surplus in 2019.▪ The allocation does not make the flying worthless, because neither cargo nor loyalty exists without the network. It does mean the marginal dollar of operating income is a loyalty or cargo dollar, and that a fare environment one to two points weaker removes the operating profit.

Q2-2026 is a clean test of which lines move with capacity, because capacity rose 3.5%, passengers 5.4% and the fuel price 79.4%. Depreciation rose 4.0%, maintenance 4.7% and salaries 6.2%; other operating rose 8.6% and landing fees 9.9%, both faster than seat-miles because they scale with passengers and departures; distribution rose 32.2% because it scales with revenue dollars and reflects credit-card fees; aircraft rent rose 67.2% on sale-leaseback conversions; fuel rose 84.1% on a 2.7% increase in gallons (10-Q Q2-2026). Fuel burn was 0.0140 gallons per ASM in Q2-2026 against 0.0141 a year earlier and 0.0151 in FY2019, a 7.3% improvement in six years from newer aircraft and larger gauge.

Realised operating leverage. Over the three years to 2025, revenue rose $14,115m and non-fuel operating expense rose $13,455m, so 4.7 cents of each incremental dollar reached operating income before any fuel effect; in 2024-2025 the same calculation is negative 37.0%.▪ Management measures the same thing as CASM-ex, which rose 0.4% in FY2025 (Q4-2025 release). Flat unit cost on 6.1% more seat-miles against PRASM down 2.9% does not produce margin, so unit-cost discipline and operating leverage are separate claims.

Labour. Pay per employee rose from $125,871 in 2019 to $155,892 in 2025, up 23.8%, while seat-miles per employee declined from 2.97m to 2.92m and salaries went from 27.9% to 29.9% of revenue (10-K FY2019 and FY2025; FY2020 five-year statistics table for 2019 headcount). Output per employee is below 2019 even though North American gauge went from 104 to 126 seats a departure over the same period.

Revenue is decomposed into volume and price, with each volume driver traced to the exposure that ultimately moves it.

Cargo International air-freight yields; belly capacity follows the passenger schedule 3.0% (3%) Cyclical Mixed. Revenue per ton mile 35.4c (2019), 71.4c (2022), 49.1c (2025), 56.5c (Q2-2026) on volume up only 8.9%

Derivation: total revenue rose $14,115m over 2022-2025, of which passenger +$13,406m, cargo -$392m and other +$1,101m. Holding PRASM at the 2022 level, the 33.3% capacity increase accounts for $13,312m of the passenger change and price for $99m.

Where a claimed driver did not appear. Pricing contributed nothing to three years of passenger revenue growth. PRASM was 16.15 cents in 2022 and 16.18 cents in 2025, and over 2023-2025 it declined from 16.84c to 16.18c, so volume contributed 150% of the passenger revenue change and price -50% (10-K FY2022 and FY2025 operating statistics).▪ The premiumisation and brand loyalty management describes shows up as mix inside a flat PRASM.

Three undisclosed quantities

Loyalty revenue. Management quotes a loyalty growth rate every quarter without a level. Travel miles redeemed inside passenger revenue plus the partner-agreement amount recognised in other operating revenue gives $6,050m for FY2024 and $6,614m for FY2025, a 9.3% increase against the "up 9%" management stated (Q4-2025 call); the same sum matches management's figures for Q1-2025 and Q2-2026 within the rounding of the $0.1bn partner disclosure. Loyalty revenue was therefore $6,614m in FY2025, 11.2% of total revenue, against $4,213m and 9.7% in 2019, a 7.8% compound rate [estimate: two disclosed GAAP lines summed, validated against three management statements].▪

Cash from third-party mile sales. The June-2020 MileagePlus financing presentation disclosed that the program received $3,803m of cash from third parties in 2019 and $1,527m from United, with $1,828m of EBITDA on a 34% margin (ir.united.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. Scaling that 2019 figure two ways — holding the 52.6% immediate-recognition share of 2019 constant, and growing the 2019 cash by the 60% increase in recognised partner revenue — both give about $6.1bn for 2025, and a check against the mile deferral comes to within 12%. Third-party mile sales therefore generated roughly $5.8-6.4bn of cash in FY2025, about 10% of revenue [estimate: the 2019 disclosed cash split scaled by recognised partner revenue, cross-checked against the frequent-flyer deferral].▪ Both routes start from the same 2019 figure, so the 10% spread understates the uncertainty. Applying the 2019 program EBITDA margin to 2025 volumes would put the program near $2.0-2.2bn of EBITDA, but that margin was struck on carve-out accounting with an intercompany redemption cost fixed at $0.01 a mile and is not a consolidated margin.

Premium revenue. Cabin-fare revenue (passenger revenue less ancillary fees and award redemptions) was $45,224m in 2025 against $44,179m in 2024, growth of 2.37%. Solving the disclosed cabin growth rates against that base gives premium revenue of roughly $18-21bn, 34-39% of passenger revenue [estimate: management's cabin growth rates solved against reported cabin-fare revenue].▪ The inputs do not agree with each other: the Q4-2025 release states premium revenue up 9% in the quarter and Basic Economy up 7% in the quarter and 5% for the year, while Nocella said on the same morning that premium was up 12% in the quarter and that standard and Basic Economy together declined about 5% for the year. Using the release figures the implied premium share is about 40% of cabin fares; using the call's Q4 figure it is about 29%. A separate disclosure puts premium seats at 27.4m, 12.3% of the roughly 222.0m seats flown, which at a 40-46% revenue share implies a blended premium-to-main fare multiple of 4.8x to 6.1x. Domestic first sells at roughly 2-3x a main-cabin fare, so the revenue metric must include Economy Plus seating and seat fees that the seat count excludes. United publishes two meanings of "premium" in the same year and reconciles neither.

Capital and working capital

Capital expenditure has run near twice depreciation for three years: $7,171m, $5,615m and $5,874m against depreciation of $2,671m, $2,928m and $2,939m, or 13.3%, 9.8% and 9.9% of revenue. Firm purchase commitments were $57,000m at YE2025, $12,600m of it contractually in 2026, against guidance of about $7.5bn of adjusted capital expenditure for 2026 (10-K FY2025, Note 12; Investor Update, 15 July 2026).

Working capital is negative and the customer funds it. Advance ticket sales and frequent-flyer deferred revenue were $15,908m at YE2025, 26.9% of revenue, and $18,723m at 30 June 2026; receivables were $2,391m, about 15 days of revenue, because customers pay by card before they fly.▪ Operating cash flow of $8,431m in 2025 was 2.51x net income. The frequent-flyer balance is 2.3 years of current travel redemptions and grew 47.4% between 2019 and 2025 against passenger revenue up 34.9%, so miles are being issued faster than they are redeemed: cash today against an obligation priced at future ticket value, which rises with fares.

2. Key technologies and technical differentiators

United's business depends on seven named platforms. Two are technology in the strict sense and neither is exclusive to United: Starlink low-earth-orbit Wi-Fi, bought from SpaceX, and the new-generation Boeing and Airbus fleet, bought from the two airframers every peer buys from. The rest are commercial systems or regulatory and geographic positions. United differentiates by how early and how widely it adopts, and by hub geography; each adoption lead has a date on which it closes.▪

Platform What it is Position against Delta and American When the lead closes
Starlink Wi-Fi LEO satellite broadband, free for MileagePlus members; 450 aircraft at Q2-2026, near 1,000 targeted by YE2026, whole fleet by end-2027 Both give members free Wi-Fi on geostationary systems; Delta reached its 1,000th free Wi-Fi aircraft in December 2025 and American stopped charging AAdvantage members in 2026 Southwest's first Starlink aircraft entered service 22 June 2026 with 300+ planned by year-end; JetBlue signed Amazon Leo in September 2025
Seatback screens, Signature Interior, Elevated cabins 150,000+ screens on 765 jets; Signature Interior on 68% of the narrowbody fleet, 530+ aircraft; $1.6bn of retrofit spend Delta fits screens on most mainline aircraft Retrofit completion moved from mid-2025 to 2027
New-generation fleet and gauge 737 MAX 8/9/10, 787, A321neo/XLR; 104 to 126 seats a North American departure Management put United about 150 aircraft behind the nearest competitor on 200-seat narrowbodies Closes as MAX 10 and A321 deliveries arrive from 2027
MileagePlus and the Chase card $7,777m of deferred revenue; about $3.2bn recognised from partner agreements in 2025 Delta received $8,200m from American Express in 2025 and expects $10bn Contract extended in February 2020 into 2029
App, united.com, NDC, owned reservation system 86% day-of-travel app use, 87.7% digital check-in; SHARES owned; continuous pricing live in Sabre and Amadeus Delta reacquired Deltamatic and its operations systems from Travelport in 2014 Individual features copy in one to three years
Kinective Media First-party travel-data ad network on screens, app and lounges, launched June 2024 Delta Sync is the analogue; Delta describes an onboard digital customer platform Revenue undisclosed; management targeted a doubling in 2025 and again in 2026

Sources: 10-K FY2025 Item 1 and Item 2; Q3-2025, Q4-2025, Q1-2026 and Q2-2026 releases and calls; DAL 10-K FY2025 ("we celebrated an important milestone with our 1,000th free Wi-Fi-enabled aircraft entering service"); AAL 10-K FY2025 ("in 2026, we stopped charging for Wi-Fi"); LUV 10-Q Q2-2026; JBLU 10-K FY2025.

Starlink, mechanically. SpaceX's satellites orbit at roughly 550 km and are linked by optical lasers, so an aircraft over an ocean is served without a ground station beneath it; the aviation product is specified at up to 1 Gbps down and latency "as low as 20ms" (starlink.com/aviation, accessed 2026-09-12) [web]. Geostationary satellites orbit at about 35,800 km and the round trip adds several hundred milliseconds; published comparisons put geostationary aviation latency at 600-800 ms (nextbigfuture.com, accessed 2026-09-12) [web, secondary]. The latency gap is orbital distance and no geostationary operator can engineer it away; the throughput gap narrows as higher-capacity satellites launch. The service is free to members, so United monetises it through enrolment and through Kinective advertising, neither of which is disclosed at the line-item level. The disclosed effect is on satisfaction: Wi-Fi satisfaction "nearly doubled" on equipped aircraft, and management cites a 90-plus net promoter score for in-flight service on those aircraft (Q2-2026 release; Bernstein conference, 27 May 2026). Replication needs a SpaceX contract, per-type certification and installation downtime, which is cost and schedule for a large airline. Kirby describes the advantage as timing: United "deliberately delayed launch until competitors locked in with other providers" (stratechery.com, accessed 2026-09-12) [web].

Gauge, the cost mechanism that has not arrived. A larger aircraft spreads crew, landing, gate and overhead cost over more seats. United's own 2021 arithmetic: an A321neo seats 55% more than an A319 for 13% more cost per departure, giving 27% lower CASM-ex, and incremental MAX 10 unit cost was put 48% below average domestic CASM-ex, "below 6 cents" [deck: United Next Investor Event 2021-06-29, slides 30 and 31]. Fuel cost per seat on a 700-mile stage was $36 on a 50-seat regional jet, $25 on an A319 and $16 on a MAX 9 [deck: same event, slide 32]. The fleet at YE2025 still held 141 737-800s at 21.8 years, 76 A319s at 23.9 years, 68 A320s at 25.7 years and 40 737-700s at 26.8 years (10-K FY2025, Item 2).

The order book and what has been delivered. Firm commitments were 634 aircraft at YE2025 and 581 at 30 June 2026, the difference being the 53 aircraft taken in the first half.

Type Firm at YE2025 Contractual 2026 Expected 2026 Expected 2027
787 150 48 20 26
737 MAX 9 103 103 76 27
737 MAX 10 167 3 0 21
A321neo 119 18 16 3
A321XLR 50 8 8 16
A350 45 0 0 0
Total 634 180 120 93

(10-K FY2025, Item 2.) The 737 MAX 10 is the largest single commitment and was promised in the fleet in 2023 [deck: United Next 2021-06-29, slide 14]. Boeing completed the type's final planned certification flight test in July 2026 and targets certification in 2026 with customer deliveries in 2027 (boeing.com, accessed 2026-09-12) [web]; Nocella said in July 2026 that United has "renewed optimism that we'll take delivery of our first MAX 10 in mid- to late 2027" (Q2-2026 call). The 45 A350s have no expected delivery year in either the 10-K or the 10-Q, and Rolls-Royce, whose Trent XWB is the type's only engine, terminated the 2010 widebody engine agreements in December 2025 after United demanded repayment of a $175m commitment payment made in 2017 (10-K FY2025, Note 12).

The reservation system. Kirby says United is "the only airline, I think, in the world that owns our own reservation system. We run on shares. We don't have to go through Sabre" (Bernstein conference, 27 May 2026). Delta reacquired the data and intellectual-property rights to Deltamatic and its flight-operations systems from Travelport in May 2014 and described itself then as the only US airline with direct control of those systems (travelmarketreport.com, accessed 2026-09-12) [web]. Two of the three US network carriers therefore control their passenger service system, and the barrier for the third is a multi-year migration. United's own migration off the Fortran-era SHARES code base has cost "several hundred million dollars" by one Kirby account and "close to $1 billion" including the data lake by another, both in 2026.

What third parties measure. Cirium's 2025 review put United fourth in North America on arrivals within 15 minutes at 78.77%, behind Delta at 80.90%, Alaska at 79.20% and Spirit at 78.83%▪ (cirium.com, accessed 2026-09-12) [web]. J.D. Power's 2026 study places United outside the top three in all three cabin segments (jdpower.com, accessed 2026-09-12) [web]. United's own evidence is an internal net promoter score whose level is never published, day-of-travel app use of 86% and a departure metric on which it says it ranks first among the eight largest US carriers.

Programs United executes with its own staff have shipped on or near time; programs whose input is a Boeing or Airbus delivery are two to four years late. The 2027 plan — double-digit margin, a gauge step-up, the MAX 10 entering service — depends mostly on the second kind.▪ That pattern describes the last five years: the Starlink and screen programs also consumed aircraft downtime, and the 2026 capacity cut was a fuel decision United made itself.

3. Competitive advantages and moat assessment

United does not disclose what MileagePlus earns, and the program's cash and margin can only be estimated. On the FY2025 estimates in Section 1, the program supplied something like a quarter of consolidated EBITDA of $7,652m on 11.2% of revenue, which would leave the transport operation near an 11% EBITDA margin before $2,939m of depreciation and $1,373m of interest. That arithmetic scales a 2019 carve-out margin and is quoted as a range throughout, and it is the largest open question about where United's returns come from. If it is right, the assessment below is partly an assessment of a mile-purchase contract that expires in 2029.

United earns returns above its cost of capital in the up-cycle and roughly at its cost of capital across the cycle.▪ Return on invested capital was 12.6% in 2025 against a cost of capital of about 9-10% [estimate: CAPM, with a 5.0% risk-free rate, an adjusted beta of 1.40, a 5-6% equity risk premium and a 4.7% after-tax cost of debt at 56/44 weights], and averaged 12.8% over 2023-2025. Across 2016-2025 it averaged 7.9%, an average that includes $7.5bn of federal Payroll Support Program grants booked as credits to operating expense in 2020-2021.▪ Bloomberg's own cost-of-capital field for United is 12.7%, at which the 2025 return is at or marginally below the cost of capital; at either figure the 2023-2025 conclusion holds and the ten-year conclusion fails.

The advantage is real in three places and absent in a fourth. Hub scale at Newark, Houston, Denver and San Francisco with immunised joint businesses on the Atlantic and Pacific gives United the largest international network of any US carrier at a unit cost below both network peers: CASM-ex of 12.64 cents in 2025 against 13.86 at Delta and 14.12 at American, each on its own definition.▪ MileagePlus is a growing annuity: partner revenue recognised in other operating revenue rose from $1.7bn in 2016 to $3.2bn in 2025 and deferred revenue from $4,883m to $7,777m.▪ Premium cabins are the fastest-growing revenue line, up about 11% in 2025 and 16% in Q2-2026 on 27.4m premium seats. Pricing power in the base cabin is absent: passenger unit revenue rose 16.4% from 2019 to 2025 while non-fuel unit cost rose 23.8%▪, and the 10-K says United "often find[s] it necessary to match competitors' discounted fares" and has "had limited ability" to raise fares enough to offset fuel (10-K FY2025, Item 1 and Item 1A).

Management claims: the advantages are "structural, permanent, irreversible and they're growing and it's simply not practical to copy them" (Q2-2025 call), built on hubs, gauge-driven cost, product and loyalty. The vocabulary changed before the business did: in 2018 Kirby declined the word moat, "having been deposed by the DOJ a few times"; from 2024 it appears on most calls. Operating margin was 7.8% in 2018 and 8.0% in 2025.

External sources: Delta and United accounted for more than 86% of the profits of the seven largest US airlines in 2024, and a J.P. Morgan analyst wrote that "a portion of the industry is drowning; incapable of producing profit, even during the summer peak" (cnbc.com, accessed 2026-09-12) [web]. The same article records United's Q2-2025 consolidated unit revenue down 4.5%, in the quarter management called structural. Delta's CEO describes United as "doing their best to copy us" (thepointsguy.com, accessed 2026-09-12) [web]. American earned about $3bn less than United in 2025 and has announced premium cabins, lounges, a widebody order and Starlink (cnbc.com, accessed 2026-09-12) [web].

Ground-up view: route entry is free for any DOT-certified US carrier and aircraft are portable, so the barriers that matter are at the hub. There they are high — slots at DCA, JFK and LGA, FAA hourly caps at EWR and ORD, gate leases, and connecting traffic that covers a flight's cost before a local seat is sold. International entry is set by bilateral agreements and the cabotage prohibition, and antitrust immunity permits schedule and fare coordination with Lufthansa Group, Air Canada, ANA and Air New Zealand that would otherwise be illegal. Surplus is shared: labour is 83% unionised under the Railway Labor Act and took $745m of ratification accruals across 2025-2026; Boeing and Airbus supply substantially all aircraft and set delivery timing; airports set fees on cost recovery; fuel is unhedged and was 31% of Q2-2026 operating expense. Seats are perishable and the marginal cost of filling one is near zero, which is the mechanism behind the 10-K's fare-matching sentence. The third network carrier can rebuild the same position at its own hubs, which is what American announced in July 2026.

United's parity with Delta on margin is a cost outcome: Delta earns 19% more revenue per seat-mile and spends 17% more per seat-mile.▪ Delta's reported unit revenue includes third-party refinery sales worth 1.70 cents of its 21.26-cent TRASM, so the airline-only gap to United's 17.88c is 1.68 cents.

Over time. The deficit to Delta narrowed from 4-6 points of operating margin and 5-11 points of return in 2016-2019 to about a point and zero in 2024-2025. The premium over the four domestic-focused carriers went from -1 point of return in 2019 to +11 points in 2024-2025 and widened each year from 2021 to 2024. That premium widened because those four collapsed — Southwest from 13.2% to 1.5%, Alaska from 12.1% to 2.1%, JetBlue from 9.9% to -4.1% — more than because United improved, since United's own margin went from 9.9% to 8.0%.▪ A gap that widens while the leader's own margin declines is evidence of relative cost position and revenue mix.

Where that places United

The advantage earns excess returns today and is open to erosion. The 2020-2021 losses of $9.0bn were survived with $7.5bn of government grants and a securitisation of the loyalty program; realised price has not outrun input-cost inflation in any window since 2019; and the growth plan requires $57.0bn of aircraft commitments whose delivery United does not control. It is clearly above a business with no durable edge: over 2023-2025 United's return exceeded the mean of American, Southwest, Alaska and JetBlue by 8-12 points each year, and the gap widened every year from 2021 to 2024.

Business-model analogues. Delta is the same model with a larger loyalty annuity and majority-share hubs in Atlanta, Detroit and Minneapolis; Delta's 2016-2019 return averaged 21.9% against United's 13.9% and the two converged to 12.8% and 12.6% in 2025, so United is the weaker twin on revenue quality and the equal on cost.▪ Royal Caribbean and Carnival share the shape — capacity constrained by an equipment duopoly, premium segmentation, heavy reinvestment, cyclical returns — and the analogue breaks on distribution, because a cruise line sells most inventory on its own pricing calendar without a competitor two gates away. UPS and FedEx share hub-and-spoke density economics and unionised labour, and the analogue breaks on pricing, because parcel carriers set annual rate increases on contract customers while an airline reprices every seat daily against published competitor fares.

4. Competitive landscape and market sizing

United is the scale leader in international flying and in cargo, the smallest of the big three in loyalty, and fourth of four in the US domestic market where two-thirds of industry capacity is flown.▪

Market sizing. IATA puts 2025 global industry revenue at $1.065 trillion with net profit of $23.0bn, a 2% net margin, and expects $1.165 trillion in 2026 (iata.org, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. United's $59,070m is 5.5% of the 2025 pool.

The US domestic passenger pool is built two ways. BTS reports domestic revenue passenger miles for the twelve months to May 2026 of 142.31bn for Delta at a 17.9% share, 140.24bn for American at 17.6% and 135.82bn for Southwest at 17.0%, each implying a pool of 795-799bn RPMs; at roughly 19 cents an RPM that is about $151bn [estimate: BTS domestic RPM pool at an approximate domestic yield] (transtats.bts.gov, accessed 2026-09-12) [web]. From the filings, the six US publics reported $201,555m of passenger revenue in FY2025, of which domestic is 59-71% for the network carriers and effectively all of Southwest's, giving $130-140bn, plus roughly $12bn for the low-cost carriers. The two methods bracket the pool at $145-155bn. United's domestic passenger revenue of about $31,500m (58.9% of passenger revenue per the quarterly releases) is 20-22% of that pool, and its disclosed domestic revenue of $35,017m, which is total operating revenue by region and therefore includes cargo, partner revenue and Canada-origin traffic, is 23-24%.▪ Either basis is well above the 17.0% BTS share, because BTS attributes traffic to the operating certificate and the 424 United Express aircraft appear under SkyWest, Mesa, Republic, CommuteAir and GoJet even though United sets the schedule, price and inventory (10-K FY2025, Item 1). The same distortion applies to Delta and American.

Structure. On BTS domestic RPMs the shares are Delta 17.9%, American 17.6%, Southwest 17.0%, United 17.0%, Alaska 6.8%, JetBlue 4.6%, Frontier 3.8%, Spirit 2.7%, SkyWest 2.6% and Envoy 1.2%, an HHI near 1,306, which is unconcentrated by the DOJ and FTC thresholds.▪ Two things qualify it. Regional carriers sell no seats of their own, so on a marketing-carrier basis Alaska, American, Delta and United with their affiliates supplied more than 65% of domestic capacity in both 2019 and 2025, and adding Southwest takes the top five past 80% (alpa.org, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. And airlines compete route by route: American held 66.9% of Dallas/Fort Worth enplanements and 67.9% of Charlotte's over the twelve months to May 2026, before its regional affiliates (transtats.bts.gov, accessed 2026-09-12) [web].

Who sets price. No carrier posts a price the others must take. The 10-K says: "In order to remain competitive and maintain passenger traffic levels, we often find it necessary to match competitors' discounted fares" (10-K FY2025, Item 1). Price is set by whoever will fly an unprofitable seat, which is why cost harmonisation matters more than capacity discipline in 2026.▪ Kirby's own decomposition of the Q2-2026 increase: "10% of price here in the second quarter was less capacity growth in the second and third quarter. 90% of it is the structural change that happened with cost increases" (Q2-2026 call).

Where the profit is. American, Delta and United accounted for 93% of US industry operating profit and 95% of pre-tax profit in the June 2025 quarter, and Delta and United alone were expected to produce 74% and 80% of industry operating and pre-tax profit for 2025 [web, ALPA October 2025].▪

Share counter-evidence

  • Spirit's capacity left and other carriers took it. OAG's April 2026 analysis showed Spirit's scheduled summer seats down from 23.3m in summer 2025 to 10.7m in summer 2026 (oag.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]; Spirit then ceased operations on 2 May 2026 (npr.org, accessed 2026-09-12) [web]. Across the 339 routes Spirit served in summer 2025, competitors added about 2.7m seats for June-August 2026, replacing 48% of its 5.67m seats, and "airlines have replaced about 60% of Spirit's former capacity" by September. Frontier's share of seats in those markets rose from 5.6% to 10.4%; United added about 334,000 seats and American about 299,000 (aviationweek.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web].
  • Capacity is growing again at the carriers management describes as marginal. OAG's September 2026 US schedule shows Alaska seats up 30%, Breeze up 46%, Frontier up 23% and JetBlue up 14% year over year, against United up 5% and Delta up 1%▪ (oag.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]. Alaska is the largest single contributor to that growth and is a network carrier, so the data qualifies management's framing that "ULCC capacity becomes less relevant" (Q4-2025 call) without contradicting it outright.
  • Regulatory caps limit United's growth at its two largest hubs. Newark's hourly cap was extended for another year, O'Hare's order was extended with United approved to fly 650 flights a day "almost indefinitely", and an FAA approach change at San Francisco lowered landing rates (Q2-2026 call, Nocella and Enqvist). The caps hold competitors' frequencies as well as United's, and they force United's growth into larger aircraft, which depends on the delayed deliveries.
  • JetBlue became a partner. Blue Sky links the two loyalty programs, gives United up to seven daily JFK round trips from 2027 and exchanges eight Newark timings, adding distribution in Boston and New York without adding United capacity (news.jetblue.com, accessed 2026-09-12) [web].
  • Transatlantic scale is close and United leads it narrowly. OAG's summer 2026 schedule count, published in May 2026, puts United at 9.72m transatlantic seats, Delta at 9.68m, American at 7.19m, British Airways at 6.24m, Lufthansa at 5.10m and Air France at 4.51m; across the twenty carriers in that table United holds about 14%▪ (oag.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web].

5. Value chain and profit pools

Of each dollar United collected in 2025, unionised labour received 29.9 cents, fuel suppliers 19.3 cents, airports and air traffic control 6.5 cents, engine makers and outside maintenance shops 5.6 cents, aircraft owners 5.4 cents, regional carriers 4.6 cents and distribution intermediaries 3.6 cents. United kept 8.0 cents as operating income and 5.7 cents as net income.▪ In Q2-2026 fuel took 28.9 cents and operating income was 6.2 cents.

Bargaining power moved to employees, engine makers and airport authorities.▪

The binding constraint

Candidate Evidence it binds in 2026-2027 Evidence it does not
Airframe deliveries Expected 2026 deliveries were 67% of contractual; 787s slipping; the MAX 10's first delivery hoped for July 2027; the 136-seat gauge target reached "probably a year late" Boeing's 737 rate rose from 42 to 47 a month with a fourth line started; Airbus has no aircraft awaiting airframes; United cut H2-2026 capacity for fuel economics while holding 1,552 aircraft and 29 grounded ERJ145s
Engines and engine shop capacity Pratt-powered 777s grounded for the summer of 2026 for lack of parts; the A350 order has no engine path after the Rolls-Royce termination; Airbus's ramp is paced by Pratt volumes United bought spare engines in advance; the 787/GEnx and MAX/LEAP-1B fleets are not on the affected list
Airports and ATC FAA hourly caps at EWR and ORD; the November 2025 shutdown cut schedules at about 40 airports Caps limit frequencies and not seats per departure
Fuel economics H2-2026 capacity cut to flat-to-+2%: "It simply doesn't make sense to fly marginal flights that will lose cash in a higher fuel price environment" (Q1-2026 call) Management expects to pass fuel through in full by Q4-2026

In 2026 the constraint on flown capacity is fuel economics and the FAA caps; the constraint on the fleet plan through 2028 is engine supply, which shows in United's numbers as 787 slippage, grounded 777s and a stalled A350 order.▪ Kirby: "there's still 800 or 900 aircraft around the globe that are grounded for engines... that is not getting fixed this decade" (Bernstein, 27 May 2026). Airbus said by mid-2026 that it "no longer had aircraft ready for handover but waiting solely for engines" (airwaysmag.com, accessed 2026-09-11) [web].

Customer-side economics and bargaining power

Yield rose 18.9% between 2019 and 2025 and another 12.1% in Q2-2026 with load factor up and, per the 10-Q, minimal demand effect from the higher price points. Unit fuel cost rose 2.56 cents in that quarter and unit revenue 2.19 cents, so fares covered about 85% of the unit fuel increase within one quarter. Passengers paid for the fuel and had not yet paid for the $922m of labour, airport, distribution and other inflation in the same quarter.

Interface Direction since 2019 Quantification

Engine makers and shops to United To the suppliers Maintenance 4.1% to 5.6% of revenue; GE's segment margin 23.7% (2023) to 26.6% (2025)
Airports to United To airports Landing fees and rent 5.9% to 6.5% of revenue, +30.6% per ASM; Kirby puts airport fees up about 60% since 2020
Fuel suppliers to United Market-set; refiners captured the 2026 shock Jet crack spreads from about $21-22 a barrel before the Iran conflict to $85-95 in early March 2026 (sherwood.news, accessed 2026-09-11) [web]

Distribution to United To United Distribution expense declined 5.5% in 2025 on a change in sales-channel mix and a refinement of the credit-card fee estimate; it rose 32.2% in Q2-2026 with revenue. Expedia states that it "could encounter increased pressure" on air remuneration as carriers shift to direct-connect technology (EXPE 10-K FY2025)
United to passengers Toward United in 2026 Yield +12.1% with load factor up; five fare increases and a bag-fee increase since late March
United to Chase Toward United at renewal The contract runs into 2029 and is in its "sunset phase" with renegotiation not started (Q2-2026 call)

Sizing the partner cash. United recognised $3,200m in other operating revenue from partner agreements in 2025 and deferred $3,883m of miles earned, which includes flight-earned miles. If flight-earned miles are 35-50% of the deferral, partner-sold miles are $1,900-2,500m and total partner cash is $5,100-5,700m, 8.6-9.7% of revenue [estimate: recognised partner revenue plus the partner share of miles deferred]. Delta's American Express remuneration was $8,200m, 12.9% of revenue, and American's cash from co-brand and other partners $6,200m, 11.3%. At Delta's ratio United would collect about $7,600m, so closing that gap is worth $1,900-2,500m a year.▪ The three carriers report on three different bases.

Circular financing

United held $3,506m of purchase deposits with the airframers at YE2025 while Boeing held $59,404m of customer advances across all customers and $25,600m of deferred production cost to be recovered from future deliveries, and Boeing in turn offers United backstop financing on some deliveries. Lessors fund part of United's fleet and pay for scarce delivery positions: 63 sale-leasebacks did not qualify as sales and remain on the balance sheet with $4,368m of future payments, while the qualifying transactions produced $1,223m of gains in eighteen months. The loyalty program financed the airline in 2020 and is now unencumbered, the term loan prepaid in July 2024 and the notes redeemed in July 2025. United finances its own regional suppliers, owning 196 of the 424 CPA aircraft and holding 194 call options, and it paid Republic a non-refundable $49m to cover Mesa-merger costs. Airport and fuel infrastructure is financed on United's credit: $2.8bn of guaranteed special facility revenue bonds and $513m of contingent exposure to fuel-consortium loans (10-K FY2025, Notes 11 and 12).

6. Secular and industry trends

Growth attribution. United's passenger revenue rose 34.9% from 2019 to 2025. Capacity contributed 15.9%, yield 18.9% and load factor -2.1%, and the product of the three reproduces the reported figure. Price did more than volume over six years; over the last three years volume did all of it.▪

United's growth against its own plan, the industry and the peer cohort:

  • Its own ultimate volume driver. United's seat-miles grew 2.5% a year from 2019 to 2025 against a 4-6% plan, and its traffic 2.1% a year.
  • Industry dollars and industry volume. US-carrier capacity grew 1.8% a year and traffic 1.2% a year over the same window, so United gained share: 22.9% to 23.9% of US-carrier ASMs and 22.7% to 23.9% of RPMs (BTS T-100 via FRED, accessed 2026-09-12) [web]. In 2025 US domestic traffic declined 0.4% while domestic capacity rose 2.1%, and IATA reports US domestic traffic -0.6% on capacity +1.7%, "the sharpest regional decline" (iata.org, accessed 2026-09-12) [web].
  • The peer cohort. Revenue CAGRs 2019-2025: United 5.3%, Delta 5.1%, Southwest 3.8%, American 3.0%, JetBlue 1.9%. United matched Delta's revenue growth with roughly twice Delta's capacity growth and three points more unit-revenue growth, and Delta's margin is still a point higher. The domestic-focused cohort lost 4 to 14 points of operating margin between 2019 and 2025.

The share gain is predominantly international. United's domestic capacity share was about 18.4% in 2019 and 18.5% in 2025, while its share of US-carrier international capacity rose from about 34% to about 36%▪ [estimate: 2019 regional capacity weights chosen so the weighted regional indices reproduce the reported 2025 total; the domestic share is reliable to about half a point]. By region, 2025 passenger revenue against 2019 = 100 was Domestic 126.8, Atlantic 158.9, Pacific 134.6 and Latin America 144.5, and the four indices applied to the 2025 regional mix reproduce 2019 regional revenue to within $15m.

The claimed secular drivers. Premiumisation appeared, and it is the reason unit revenue did not decline further: premium revenue rose about 11% in 2025 on 7% more premium capacity in Q4 while main cabin rose 1% on 6% more capacity. Loyalty appeared: other operating revenue rose 56.9% from 2019 to 2025 against passenger revenue up 34.9%. Gauge as a cost driver did not: CASM-ex is 12.64 cents against the 2021 plan's 9.4 cents for 2026. International structural change has appeared so far: Atlantic unit revenue is 21% above 2019 and Pacific 27%, against domestic at 15%, though both Atlantic and Latin unit revenue declined in 2024-2025 as capacity was restored.

The real-fare claim. Kirby says airfares are 13% below 2019 in real terms (Q2-2026 call) and said 27% in Q1-2026. Both statements describe the CPI airline-fare index, which is 23.4% below 2019 in real terms for 2025 and 11.9% below for January-August 2026. United's own realised yield is 5.6% below 2019 in real terms for 2025 and, at Q2-2026's +12.1%, about 3% above 2019 in real terms▪ [estimate: the 2025 yield grown by the reported quarterly increase against CPI-U]. Every one of the six US carriers is within 15% of 2019 on realised yield in real terms and United is within 6%. The catch-up implied by the CPI framing applies to the industry's lowest fares and much less to United's.

The 2026 reset, and how much of it survives. The Q2-2026 repricing is a cost shock passed into fares. Jet fuel doubled after the conflict with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the four largest carriers cut about 5% of Q2-Q3 capacity and Spirit's liquidation removed about 1.4-2% of US domestic seats for May-December 2026 [web]. Management's own numbers on retention run in two directions. In April 2026 Kirby said that if fuel returned to mid-February levels United would "keep 20% of the price increase next year", adding that the longer the high price lasts the more likely the increase holds. In July he said 90% of the second-quarter increase reflected cost inflation every carrier pays and only 10% was at risk. The two are different quantities, conditioned on fuel normalising and on capacity returning. The first works out as 12 points of unit revenue on a $68bn base, about $7bn annualised, so giving back 80% removes about $6bn, close to the incremental 2026 fuel bill of "almost $6 billion" (Q2-2026 call).

Consensus assumes the reset holds: FY2027 revenue of $71,183m is 4.8% above FY2026 and implies an operating margin of 9.8%.

Policy and technology shifts

Shift Mechanism Timing Direction

What would show first if the case were breaking:

  • Premium unit revenue converging with main cabin for two quarters with fuel normal.
  • Hub local share flat in the quarterly DOT origin-destination data management cites.
  • Co-brand accounts or card spend growing slower than capacity.
  • Contracted business revenue turning negative while leisure holds.
  • International unit revenue negative on rising capacity across Atlantic and Pacific at once.
  • Load factor below 82% with unit revenue negative, which is what the 2025 oversupply looked like.
  • Yields giving back more than 20% of the 2026 increase within two quarters of fuel normalising.
  • CASM-ex above +3% with gauge growth resuming.
  • The frequent-flyer deferred balance ceasing to build.

7. Critical points

1. The flying does not cover its fully-allocated cost, and every dollar of operating income comes from cargo and mile sales. FY2025 passenger revenue of $53,438m was $918m below total operating expense of $54,356m; cargo of $1,779m plus other revenue of $3,853m is what produced $4,713m of operating income. The same test was positive by $667m in 2019 and has been negative in every year since. The swing is 3.4 points of passenger revenue in six years. The allocation does not make the network worthless, because neither cargo nor loyalty exists without it. It does mean the marginal dollar of profit is a cargo or loyalty dollar and that one to two points of fare weakness removes the operating profit.

2. Three years of revenue growth were seat-miles at unchanged unit revenue, and the supply of seat-miles is now constrained. PRASM was 16.15 cents in 2022 and 16.18 cents in 2025, so 99% of the $13,406m passenger-revenue increase was capacity. That capacity now arrives at 120 aircraft expected against 180 contractual for 2026, with 167 firm MAX 10s uncertified, 45 A350s with no expected delivery year, and FAA hourly caps at the two largest hubs. Management has said 2025 was "United's high watermark on domestic capacity growth" and plans to retire at least 80 aircraft in 2027.

3. The 2026 fuel shock reversed the sign on that driver within two quarters. In Q2-2026 price supplied 79% of the passenger-revenue increase and volume 21%. Yield rose 12.1%, every region priced double digits, and capacity growth halved to 3.5%. The cause is a fuel price up 79.4% to $4.19 a gallon on an unhedged book, and management is explicit that the fare increase is cost-push: "Cost inflation is what is driving fares higher" (Q2-2026 call). Revenue rose $2,436m and fuel expense $2,335m, but total operating expense rose $2,665m, so operating income declined $229m.

4. Unit cost is 23.8% above 2019 against a plan of 8% below, and the gauge increase that was supposed to fix it is late. CASM-ex was 10.21 cents in 2019 and 12.64 cents in 2025. The 2021 plan assigned 2.0 cents of its 2.8 cents of offsets to gauge and asset utilisation [deck: United Next 2021-06-29, slide 33]. Gauge reached 126 seats a North American departure against a goal restated from 134 to 136, and the aircraft that closes the gap is uncertified. Management's position is that the benefit is still ahead: "we really have not benefited from gauge yet" (Q4-2025 call).

5. Operating leverage has not existed for three years. Over 2022-2025 non-fuel operating expense rose $13,455m against a revenue increase of $14,115m, a 4.7% ex-fuel flow-through; in 2024-2025 it was negative 37.0%. A 10% pre-tax margin on FY2025 revenue is $5,907m against the $4,306m reported, a $1,601m gap equal to 0.48 cents of unit revenue. That requires a TRASM-to-CASM spread of about 1.91 cents; the widest spread in the 2019-2025 record is 1.64 cents.▪

6. Loyalty is the fastest-growing profit line and its price is contracted until 2029. Loyalty revenue compounded 7.8% a year from $4,213m in 2019 to $6,614m in 2025, and the drivers management cites are all volume: co-brand accounts +22% and card spend +14% in Q2-2026. The Chase agreement was last restated in February 2020 and extends into 2029, and Nocella confirms "a legacy contract that continues with our banking partners regarding core economics" (Q4-2025 call). On the estimated $5,100-5,700m of total partner cash, each 10% improvement in the per-mile price would be worth $510-570m at almost no incremental cost, and none of it is available before the renewal. MileagePlus is also the smallest of the big three programs on both deferred balance and recognised revenue.

7. Reported earnings are being supported by asset sales. Special charges swung from a $949m net charge in FY2023 to a $259m net charge in FY2025 and to a $534m net credit in H1-2026, which includes $796m of aircraft sale-leaseback gains. Reported Q2-2026 operating income declined 17.3% year over year; excluding special items it declined 46.3%, from $1,772m to $951m. On a trailing-twelve-month basis reported operating income is 3.4% above FY2025 and the ex-special figure is 14.3% below.▪

8. Per-share results lag the enterprise results by the 2020 equity. Revenue is 36.5% above 2019 and GAAP pre-tax income 10.0% above, but adjusted EPS of $10.62 in 2025 is 11.9% below 2019's $12.05 because diluted shares rose 26.4% to 328.5m. Ten years of repurchases cost $8,490m gross and $5,855m net of equity sold, and shares outstanding finished the decade 2.8% higher than they started. Of the $3.44 of EPS growth from 2016 to 2025, $2.45 is the corporate tax rate declining from 40.8% to 22.1%.

9. Consensus asks for a margin move that few airline-years have delivered. Consensus puts FY2027 operating margin at 9.8% against FY2025's 8.0%, a 1.8-point gain two years after a fuel spike; across the eleven observations of the two prior spikes the median outcome was 0.9 points below the pre-spike margin and seven of eleven ended lower. Measured from the H1-2026 run-rate of 6.5% the required move is 3.3 points, beyond every observation in that set. No US carrier has reached a 10% operating margin since 2021, and United has cleared a 10% pre-tax margin twice in eighteen years, in 2015 and 2016, at fuel under $2.00 a gallon.▪

10. The balance sheet is where the record supports the forecast. Debt principal came down $12.5bn from the 2021 peak to $21,383m at YE2025, the loyalty program has been unencumbered since July 2025, liquidity was $19.6bn at 30 June 2026 against a $2.0bn covenant minimum, and five rating upgrades in thirteen months took United to one notch below investment grade at S&P and Fitch. Net leverage was 2.2x at each of the last two year-ends and 2.2x again at 30 June 2026 after dipping to 2.0x at 30 June 2025, and the improvement management described between the Q4-2024 call and the FY2025 release is the 1 January 2025 redefinition of adjusted EBITDAR.

Items 4, 5, 6 and 9 are also management-claim pressure tests and are argued in full in Section 8.

8. Management claim pressure tests

"Structural, permanent, irreversible." Kirby, Q2-2025: "the advantages that we have are structural, permanent, irreversible and they're growing and it's simply not practical to copy them." Ten-year return on invested capital averaged 7.9% including $7.5bn of government grants; operating margin was 11.9% in 2016, 9.9% in 2019, 8.0% in 2025 and 6.2% in Q2-2026, four quarters after the statement. The company's own 10-K describes the mechanism the calls deny: "we often find it necessary to match competitors' discounted fares", and the company "historically has had limited ability to, and may not be able to in the future, increase its fares and fees sufficiently to offset the full impact of increases in fuel prices" (10-K FY2025, Item 1 and Item 1A). American announced in July 2026 that it would rebuild the same premium, lounge, widebody and connectivity position at its own hubs.

"Cost convergence is permanent." Kirby, Q2-2026: "Perhaps the most important structural change in the industry has been the significant inflation and harmonization in nonfuel costs like airport fees, labor, and maintenance." United's own non-fuel unit cost rose 23.8% between 2019 and 2025, faster than its unit revenue, and 2025 CASM-ex of 12.64 cents is above Alaska's 11.42 and JetBlue's 11.2 while below Delta's 13.86 and American's 14.12. United's 1,488-mile stage length against Southwest's 780 accounts for part of the 0.26-cent gap to Southwest, and the low-cost carriers' cost inflation is largely labour contracts that reset each cycle. Convergence as of 2025 is a fact and its permanence is a forecast.

A 10% pre-tax margin in 2027, mid-teens beyond. Leskinen, Q2-2026: "Our confidence in our ability to deliver double-digit pretax margins in 2027 and mid-teen pretax margins beyond that has never been higher." Kirby on the same call put the second half on a condition: mid-teens "requires or is likely to require some more structural changes in the industry" whose timing he declined to predict. Across 103 US airline-years since 2008, 22.3% cleared a 10% pre-tax margin and 9.7% cleared 14%, and all ten mid-teens observations fall in 2015-2018 with jet fuel between $1.25 and $2.03 a gallon. United's own maximum is 11.1%, in 2015.▪ The same target set in June 2021 for 2026 was about 14%; it moved to "update at Investor Day" in January 2024, then to double-digit without a year, then to 2027, and no filing or release retires the original.▪

A doubling of loyalty EBITDA. Kirby, Bernstein 2026: "We've got a great partnership with Chase, but it's a decade old. And the other deals have been modernized... We do expect to double the EBITDAR in that particular business." United recognises $3,200m a year from partner agreements, chiefly but not solely the Chase co-brand (10-K FY2025, Note 2), and total partner cash is estimated at $5,100-5,700m, 8.6-9.7% of revenue, against Delta's 12.9% and American's 11.3% on their own different bases. Closing the gap to Delta's ratio is worth $1,900-2,500m a year. Renegotiation had not started as of the Q2-2026 call, the contract runs into 2029, and the base against which a doubling would be measured has never been disclosed.▪ Two regulatory items point the other way: the Credit Card Competition Act and the DOT inquiry into the four largest loyalty programs, opened in September 2024 with no announced outcome.

Fuel pass-through of 100% by Q4-2026, and retention afterwards. Management reported recovering "approximately half" of the Q2-2026 fuel increase, with 80-90% expected in Q3 and full recovery in Q4. Measured year over year the revenue increase of $2,436m exceeded the fuel increase of $2,335m, and in unit terms fares covered 85% of the unit fuel increase; management measures against an unpublished internal plan it describes as "almost $6 billion higher for the year". Both figures are disclosed and they are not the same quantity. On what survives a fuel retracement the CEO has published two numbers: 20% retained (April 2026, conditioned on fuel returning to mid-February levels) and 90% retained (July 2026, conditioned on capacity, with 10% "sort of at risk").▪ Each point of 2027 unit revenue is worth roughly $1.70 of adjusted EPS [estimate: a point of TRASM on consensus 2027 revenue, taxed at 22% with a profit-sharing offset, over 325m shares], so the span between those two figures is roughly $12 of EPS against a consensus of $15.06.

Gauge as an idiosyncratic cost tailwind. The 2021 plan put gauge at 134 seats a departure by 2026 and CASM-ex 8% below 2019. Gauge is 126 and CASM-ex is 23.8% above 2019, a miss of about 32 points against the plan's own base. Management's current framework is 3-4% industry inflation offset by about a point a year from gauge and a point from core efficiency, less a point of customer investment, for 2-3% annual CASM-ex growth. Every part of that depends on aircraft whose delivery dates have moved four years.

"Our technology is now without question, the best of any airline in the world and by a wide margin" (Kirby, Q3-2024). Third-party measures do not show it. Cirium's 2025 review ranks United fourth in North America on arrivals within 15 minutes, 2.1 points behind Delta on a similar flight count, and J.D. Power's 2026 study places United outside the top three in all three cabin segments. United's supporting evidence is an internal net promoter score whose level is not published, app usage of 86% and a departure metric on which it ranks itself first. The reservation-system claim is narrower than stated: Delta reacquired control of its own systems in 2014, so two of the three network carriers own their passenger service system.

"United guides conservatively and beats." That is true by quarter and false by year. Fifteen quarterly adjusted-EPS guides since Q4-2022 produced thirteen results at or above the range, eleven consecutive inside or above, and a mean beat of about $0.14, or $0.25 excluding the Q1-2023 miss, against a typical $0.50 range width. The January full-year guide produced two beats (2018, 2019), two hits (2023, 2024), one break (2025, $0.88 below the floor) and one live year cut twice (2026, from $12-14 to $7-11 to $9-11). The quarterly guide is set two to three weeks into a quarter that is largely booked; the annual guide is set thirteen months out and has not survived an external shock in either of the last two years.

"Record" 2025. Revenue of $59,070m and 181m passengers were records. Adjusted EPS of $10.62 was 11.9% below 2019 on 26.4% more shares, GAAP pre-tax margin was 7.3% against 9.0%, and return on invested capital of 13.4% was below 2016's 16.4% and down from 15.0% in 2024.

Consensus, tested the same way. The street models operating income recovering from $4,820m in 2026 to $6,943m in 2027 and $7,886m in 2028, margins of 7.1%, 9.8% and 10.5%. Consensus revenue and the model in Section 17 agree within about a point in all three years, so the difference is entirely the incremental margin on that revenue: consensus implies a 65% incremental operating margin in 2027, the 80th percentile of 41 US airline-years with revenue growth between 2% and 10% from a positive base, and of the eight observations at or above that level, five are carriers in 2015 alone, when Gulf Coast jet spot declined 43.5%▪. Consensus 2027 operating expense also implies fuel near $3.50 a gallon, about 6% below 2026 and 43% above 2025. The two consensus lines hold together only inside a narrow fuel band: below it, management's own retention framing gives part of the fare increase back and revenue undershoots; above it, the margin does.

The five inflections

  • September 2015 to January 2018, management reset and the pivot from shrinking to growing. United had shrunk in its own hubs by a cumulative 8% over five years while Delta and American grew, and 33% of North American departures were single-class 50-seat regional jets. The board replaced the CEO in 2015 and the commercial and finance leadership in 2016, then re-based the plan on growth in January 2018 against explicit investor objection at the event. Capacity grew 4.9% in 2018 and 3.5% in 2019, PRASM rose 4.3% and 1.5% after three years of decline, and adjusted EPS went $6.85 to $9.13 to $12.05. The margin gap to Delta narrowed only from 4.9 points to 4.2; the position against American went from 1.5 points behind in 2015 to 3.2 ahead in 2019.
  • February 2020 to January 2021, COVID, forced and handled early. Over one weekend in February 2020 management concluded the virus would spread worldwide and cut capacity, capital spending and the buyback before any peer. Cash burn was held to $40m a day in Q2 and $33m in Q4; over $26bn of liquidity was raised including the first loyalty-backed financing of its kind; diluted shares rose from 259.8m to 321.9m and equity declined from $11,531m to $5,029m. United kept every widebody type, and those aircraft flew the 2022-2023 international recovery that produced today's Atlantic and Pacific position.
  • June 2021 to April 2024, United Next, ordered at the trough and then reshaped. 270 aircraft ordered with explicit 2023 and 2026 targets. The 2023 cost target was withdrawn in January 2023; 2025 CASM-ex is 24% above 2019 against a plan of 8% below; the margin target moved to 2027. In April 2024 management levelled deliveries at about 100 narrowbodies a year, converted MAX 10 positions through 2027 into MAX 9s and said it would schedule only about 90% of expected deliveries. The binding constraint turned out to be supplier delivery and the response was to under-schedule.
  • August 2024 to April 2025, capital returns resume and the brand-loyal framing takes over. Unprofitable domestic capacity began to exit in August 2024; the board authorised $1.5bn of repurchases in October with net leverage at 2.7x; $10.1bn of debt was repaid during 2024. The stock rose 135% in 2024 and 15% in 2025. Repurchases were $162m and $637m against $4.2bn in 2014-2016.
  • March to July 2026, the fuel shock and the first live test of the resilience claim. Fuel doubled; United pulled Tel Aviv and Dubai flying, cut second-half capacity to flat-to-+2% from a schedule sold in at about +4%, took five fare increases and a bag-fee increase, raised $3.7bn of precautionary bank debt with $19.6bn already on hand, and cut then partly restored the annual guide. Q2-2026 recovered 50% of the fuel increase on management's basis and 85% of the unit increase on the reported figures. The 2020 sequence repeated at smaller scale.

How management has behaved. Capacity is the first thing cut, close-in, with the unit-cost consequence accepted. Liquidity is raised before it is needed and at scale. Guidance is reset early, with scenarios in April 2025 and a policy change in July 2026. Buybacks stop in a shock and restart only inside a leverage target. Labour contracts are settled at industry-leading rates with large ratification payments and management accepts 2-3 points of CASM-ex a cycle. Multi-year targets are issued, and when the arithmetic behind one fails the target is replaced without a stated retraction: the 2016 plan's $3.8bn value figure is not referenced after January 2018, and the 2021 plan's 14% margin has no closing statement.

What the plan pays for

Kirby's 2025 target pay was $20,700,000 with 94% at risk: salary $1.2m, short-term incentive target $3.0m, performance RSUs $8.25m and time-vested RSUs $8.25m. The cash plan is one-third relative adjusted EBITDAR margin against an unnamed peer set, one-third net promoter score on an internal survey with undisclosed thresholds, and one-third operational excellence (on-time departures with connection holds counted as on-time, mishandled bags, seat-cancel rate), also with undisclosed thresholds. The performance RSUs are 40% absolute adjusted EPS, 40% relative adjusted pre-tax margin and 20% strategic technology measures, with an $8bn liquidity hurdle at the end of the period.

(2026 proxy.) Absolute adjusted EPS is the single per-share measure and is 40% of half the long-term award, about 16% of the CEO's target pay [estimate: 0.4 x $8.25m / $20.7m]. No measure in either program references return on capital, free cash flow, leverage or share count, though the CFO names free cash flow and investment grade as the priorities. Ten completed performance-RSU cycles since the 2016 grants have all paid at or above target, with a median near 127% and four at 188% or more; the cash plan paid 139%, 175% and 135% for 2023-2025. The two sub-target outcomes in the cash plan are 2018, when the financial half paid 67%, and 2020, when nothing was paid and the CEO and President waived 82% and 70% of salary.

The measures pull apart when peers are weak. In 2025 the absolute EPS test paid below target and the relative margin test paid 157%, in a year when the company's own 2021 plan implied about $20 of EPS for 2026. The 2026 fuel shock, which roughly halved quarterly earnings, reaches only the 40% absolute-EPS weight; the relative margin and relative EBITDAR measures pay against a peer average that declined with fuel, in a year when Kirby expects "4 of the 8 publicly traded commercial airlines are probably going to lose money."

Two award episodes drew objections. The September 2022 Transformation Incentive Awards paid 132% on a single measure, pilots hired and trained as a multiple of the 2013-2018 average. The July 2024 Retention LTI Awards granted $25.5m of target value across five officers, with the first two of three tranches earned on positive adjusted EPS over a trailing four-quarter window, a test cleared in every such window since 2022; the stated reason was that the CEO's realisable pay was "significantly below the levels of Chief Executive Officers at our peer companies", in a year the stock rose 135% and compensation actually paid reached $96.7m. Say-on-pay support was 86.3% in 2025, the second-lowest result on record after 82% at the 2021 meeting, and the 2026 proxy describes it as continued strong support while recording that stockholders "expressed concerns regarding the special retention LTI awards that we granted in July 2024."

The benchmarking group has nineteen companies of which three are airlines, after the 2025 addition of American Express, Booking, Nike, PayPal, Starbucks and Uber "to better reflect United's evolving business model that relies more heavily on specialty branding and competitive advantages offered by a leading digital technology platform."

Ownership and dealing. All eighteen directors and officers together hold under 1% of the shares. Kirby held 841,122 shares directly after 25 July 2026, about $92m at $109.82, plus 306,865 options struck at $110.21. Between December 2023 and August 2026 every current named officer sold and none bought in the open market: Kirby sold 120,000 shares at $107.86 in December 2025, about $6m in June 2026 and 159,321 option shares for $18.8m gross in July 2026 as a 2016 grant expired; Hart, Nocella, Enqvist, Leskinen and Gebo all sold between May and August 2026 at $107-118, after the January guide had been cut twice. The company repurchased at an average $66 in Q2-2025, when the CFO described the shares as below intrinsic value.

Candor. Operational and forecasting errors are acknowledged by name and with a figure: Flight 3411 ("I take full responsibility for making this right"), the 2018 operational bonus lottery ("our change to the operational bonus plan was a mistake, and it's my responsibility"), the Q1-2023 guidance miss ("We had a bad forecast, and we own it. We missed it"), the private flight during the 2023 Newark disruption ("It was a mistake"), and the Q1-2026 domestic call ("I thought that the domestic would be quicker to move than international, and I was wrong"). Shortfalls are attributed to weather, air traffic control, Boeing, fuel and macro uncertainty, each time with a number attached and each time paired with a statement that the plan is working. No call or conference over the decade includes an acknowledgement that a strategic target was wrong. The Investor Day intended to reset the 2021 targets was promised for May 2024, postponed, reframed in January 2025 on the basis that "our investor calls are much closer to many Investor Days", and by April 2026 described as "Maybe we'll do an Investor Day someday."

Per-share outcomes. Revenue per share rose 62.5% from 2016 to 2025 because the share count is flat across the decade. 11. M&A, divestitures and deal track record

United is not a serial acquirer and it has not destroyed capital through whole-company M&A. It has bought one business of consequence in sixteen years, the all-stock Continental merger closed on 1 October 2010, plus a Phoenix flight school in 2020 at an undisclosed price.▪ Where capital has been lost is the minority-stake and partner-loan book: about $1.1bn of disclosed cash went into Azul, the Avianca ownership chain, ExpressJet's parent and Mesa between 2015 and 2023, with a further $100m subscribed into the reorganised Azul in February 2026, and $925m of that has been recognised as losses.▪ The discipline on whole companies is real and documented: United abandoned the Newark slot transaction when the Justice Department sued in 2015-16, declined to bid for JetBlue on the arithmetic, and ended its approach to American within days of a public refusal in April 2026.

The merger cannot be graded from the goodwill line. The $4,523m has never been impaired, but United is a single reporting unit, so the annual test compares the whole company's fair value with its book equity: $35.7bn of market capitalisation against $16,697m of book equity at 30 June 2026 leaves a $19bn cushion, and the test could only fail if the equity market value declined below book. The synergy and charge record does bear on it: $400m reported once against a $1.0-1.2bn target, the target's date removed a year later, reporting discontinued the year after that, and $2,181m of integration and merger charges. The chief executive of the day received $4.5m for meeting merger metrics, paid in late 2013 and early 2014 [web].

Cumulative unrealised gains and losses on the whole equity-securities book, which also holds Archer, Eve and Clear, were -$5m, +$153m, -$194m, -$34m, +$20m, +$27m, -$199m and +$4m for 2018-2025, a net -$228m, and with the $697m credit loss that is $925m of recognised losses. The one holding that worked was received for a bankruptcy claim.

What changed in the language. The FY2016 through FY2019 risk factors stated that "An important part of our strategy to expand our global network includes making significant investments in airlines in other parts of the world." The FY2020 10-K restated it in the past and conditional: the strategy "has included making significant investments... In the future, our regional and global business strategy could include entering into JBAs, commercial agreements and strategic alliances with other carriers, and possibly making loan transactions with, and non-controlling investments in, such carriers." No new loan to a foreign partner airline has been disclosed since; United did lend to Mesa from December 2022, and the FY2023 and FY2024 10-Ks describe "several loans to Mesa" alongside the 10% equity interest.

On consolidation. Kirby's position in March 2025 was that "mergers are so hard. They're disruptive. Your technology team spends two years on the sideline... we don't need a deal for sure." In February 2026 he raised a combination with American with a White House official; American refused publicly and United withdrew on 27 April 2026. At Bernstein a month later: "the big transaction required a willing partner, which we clearly don't have. So I don't think that United at least is going to participate in any consolidation for any time I can see in the foreseeable future." On JetBlue, twice on the record: "we got to somehow think we can improve JetBlue's margin by 25 points to make it work. Like that seems mathematically close to impossible to me."

The $76m residual is the 10-Q's rounding of $3.9bn of borrowings and $4.2bn of payments.] About $18.5bn, or 80%, is secured on aircraft, routes, slots and gates, and the undrawn $3.0bn revolver shares the route, slot and gate collateral. The three unsecured pieces rank behind all of that. There is no holding-company subordination, because both 2026 issues are UAL obligations guaranteed by United.

Five actions moved the stack in the first half of 2026: $1.0bn of 5.375% notes due 2031 issued on 2 February; the 2024 Term Loan margin cut 25bp on 3 February; $1.0bn of 4.875% notes due 2029 issued on 6 February; the $2.0bn 4.375% secured notes redeemed on 24 February; and $3.9bn of aircraft-secured bank loans drawn, $3.7bn of it in Q2. United also prepaid $600m of the PSP note due 2030 in June and $500m of aircraft debt.

Cost of debt. Principal-weighted, with floating legs marked at the 3.62% Term SOFR fix, the stack costs about 5.0% [estimate: $1,152m of annual interest on $23,157m of principal]. Realised cash interest is 5.1%: FY2025 interest expense of $1,373m on an average balance of $26,822m, and H1-2026 interest of $665m annualises to 5.2% on $25,726m. Management gives 4.7% at the end of 2025 without stating a basis, consistent with a year-end coupon on debt alone that excludes the $3,249m of failed-sale-leaseback obligations priced at 5.8% and $474m of finance leases at 5.3%. Marginal cost is about 5.0% on new secured bank debt and 4.875-5.375% on the February unsecured issues, which yielded 5.82% and 5.97% in September. Including operating leases at their 6.0% discount rate, the blended cost of all interest-bearing and lease obligations is about 5.2%. Three disclosed changes push it up: the PSP notes stepping from 1.00% to SOFR plus 2.00% adds roughly $78m a year on $1.7bn of PSP2 and PSP3 principal [estimate], the 2026 bank loans price above the 2025 book and reprice quarterly, and the two 2026 bond issues replaced a 4.375% secured note.

The 2029 requirement grew by $1,820m in six months because the new unsecured notes mature alongside the 4.625% secured notes and part of the new bank debt. At $4,752m, 2029 is more than double any other year before 2031, and 48% of the stack falls after 2030. Refinancing 2029 at the September yields on United's own unsecured paper against a blended embedded coupon near 4.75% would add about $55m a year [estimate: $4,752m x (5.9% - 4.75%)].

Covenants. A $2.0bn minimum unrestricted liquidity test at all times, met with $19.6bn at 30 June 2026, and a 1.6-to-1.0 collateral coverage test assessed semi-annually, with customary negative covenants and cross-default provisions. Credit-card processors hold the right to require a reserve against processed but unflown tickets and to demand collateral if liquidity drops below stated minimums; advance ticket sales were $10,752m at 30 June 2026, which is the mechanism by which a liquidity squeeze would compound.

Operating lease obligations rose 19% in six months. The weighted-average remaining operating lease term is 11 years at a 6.0% discount rate; 63 aircraft under sale-leasebacks did not qualify as sales and stay on the balance sheet with $4,368m of future payments. Approximately $6.6bn of rental obligations for leases signed but not commenced is not on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet; those leases commence between 2026 and 2028 with terms of up to 28 years and cover mainline aircraft, regional aircraft under capacity-purchase agreements, the Houston terminal lease and office space. United also guarantees about $2.8bn of airport special facility revenue bonds and has $513m of contingent exposure to fuel-consortium loans.

Each sale-leaseback converts an owned aircraft financed with debt into an operating lease: GAAP debt declines, the operating lease liability rises, and the gain is booked in operating income as a special credit. Gains were $427m in FY2025 and $796m in H1-2026 against $1,504m of half-year net income. Management's own adjusted total debt measure counts the operating lease liability, so the figure reported to the rating agencies takes no benefit while the GAAP debt line does.

Pension

The pension plans were $577m underfunded at YE2025 on a $4,624m obligation and other postretirement benefits $495m underfunded, $1,072m combined, against $1,074m of non-current liability on the June 2026 balance sheet. Employer contributions stepped from $5m in 2024 to $298m in 2025. A 100bp decline in the discount rate would add $796m to the pension obligation, 17.2% of it, and $87m to annual cost. The expected long-term return assumed for 2026 is 8.07%, above the 7.81% used for 2025, against actual returns of 3.7% in 2024 and 9.9% in 2025.

Share-based compensation was $148m in 2025, 0.25% of revenue and 4.4% of net income, and outstanding restricted units are 1.2% of the count, so equity compensation moves the share count about a point a year. The dilution that matters came from the 2020-2021 equity and the Treasury warrants: $10,062m of repurchases from 2014 through H1-2026 against $2,635m of equity sold is $7,427m net for a 49.9m reduction in shares, about $149 a net share retired against a $109.82 price. The warrant overhang is retired, the last 3.5m warrants having been exercised in March 2025.

Net leverage moved from 2.0x to 2.2x over the year to June 2026 on earnings alone: trailing adjusted EBITDAR declined $979m, or 10.5%, while adjusted net debt declined $263m. Between June 2025 and June 2026 adjusted total debt rose $757m while GAAP debt declined $615m, the difference being $1,497m more of operating lease obligations. On Bloomberg's definitions at 11 September 2026, United's net debt to trailing EBITDA is 2.16x against Delta at 1.91x, Southwest at 1.19x, Alaska at 8.41x, American at 8.58x and JetBlue at 50.45x; on gross debt United is 4.28x, third of the six, and the gap between its gross and net measures reflects the largest cash balance in the group, $12.2bn against $31.0bn of gross debt.

The two February 2026 unsecured issues are rated Ba2 by Moody's and BB+ by S&P and Fitch. BB+ is one notch below investment grade, which matches management's statement that United is "just one notch below investment grade at all 3 agencies"; the Moody's issue rating is two notches below Baa3, which is what notching down from a Ba1 corporate family rating for an 80%-secured stack would produce, and no local source records the corporate family rating itself.

Structural risks, ordered by how much pre-tax income or reported leverage each can move

  1. Earnings volatility against a fixed charge structure. Adjusted net debt moves a few hundred million a year; trailing adjusted EBITDAR moved $979m in twelve months on fuel alone. At the June 2026 adjusted net debt, leverage reaches 2.6x if trailing EBITDAR declines to $7,000m and 3.0x at $6,000m [estimate: $18,105m over the stated EBITDAR]. EBITDA on Bloomberg's definition was negative $2,961m in 2020.
  2. The investment-grade target is arithmetically demanding. Reporting net leverage below 2.0x at 31 December 2026 with adjusted net debt held at the June level needs full-year adjusted EBITDAR above $9,053m. H1-2026 produced $3,647m, so H2 must deliver $5,406m against $4,726m in H2-2025, an increase of 14.4%▪ [estimate: FY2025 adjusted EBITDAR less the H1-2025 figure].
  3. Floating-rate exposure. $11.2bn of floating-rate debt at 30 June 2026 against $16.6bn of cash and short-term investments. The disclosed sensitivities are $63m of additional interest expense per 100bp on $8,528m of variable-rate debt and about $140m of additional interest income per 100bp on 2025 average balances, so falling rates are the net negative, by roughly $57-77m of pre-tax income per 100bp depending on whether both sides are scaled to the June balances [estimate: the two Item 7A sensitivities scaled consistently].
  4. The 2029 refinancing requirement, $4,752m, at about $55m a year of additional interest at current yields.
  5. Capital commitments larger than the debt stack. $57.0bn of firm purchase commitments, $12.6bn of it contractual in 2026, plus $19.0bn of estimated capacity-purchase payments through 2037 and about $6.6bn of signed-but-uncommenced leases, against guidance of about $7.5bn of adjusted capital expenditure for 2026. The gap between contractual and expected delivery is what keeps the near-term funding requirement manageable, and Boeing and Airbus control it.
  6. Near-term cash obligations outside the debt schedule. The flight-attendant ratification-payment liability was $742m at 30 June 2026, payable no later than 15 September 2026.
  7. Pension, at $1,072m of combined underfunding with a $796m sensitivity to 100bp of discount rate.
  8. The tax-benefits preservation plan expires on 4 December 2026. Federal net operating loss carryforwards were $10.6bn at YE2025, $10.5bn of them without expiry. The plan deters accumulations above 4.9% of the shares; once it lapses, an ownership change under Section 382 would limit their use.
  9. Effective subordination of the unsecured notes behind about $18.5bn of secured claims.
  10. Contingent guarantees: $2.8bn of special facility revenue bonds, $513m of fuel-consortium exposure and $395m of surety bonds.
