Quarterly operating cash flow and capital expenditure are derived by differencing consecutive year-to-date columns, so the seasonal pattern is real and the quarter-end cut moves with booking timing. Q1 is always the strongest cash quarter because advance ticket sales build ahead of the summer. Q4 columns for 2024 and 2025 are the full year less the nine months in that year's Q3 10-Q; the four 2025 quarters sum to $59,071m against $59,070m reported.

What drove the record

2016 to 2019, margin 11.9% to 9.9%. The unit spread narrowed 0.21 cents. Fuel cost per seat-mile rose 0.85 cents on a price that went from $1.49 to $2.09 a gallon, non-fuel unit cost was almost flat at 10.41 to 10.53 cents, and unit revenue rose 0.76 cents. Fuel explains the compression.

2019 to 2025, margin 9.9% to 8.0%. The spread narrowed 0.09 cents on a much larger base, and the composition inverted: fuel unit cost rose only 0.31 cents while non-fuel unit cost rose 2.48 cents and unit revenue 2.70 cents. The post-2019 compression is non-fuel cost, of which labour is the largest piece: salaries per seat-mile went from 4.24 to 5.34 cents while headcount grew 18.0% to 113,200 and pay per employee 23.8%.▪

2023 to 2024, margin 7.8% to 8.9%. Fuel unit cost declined 0.56 cents on a price down from $3.01 to $2.65; non-fuel unit cost rose 0.27 cents and unit revenue declined 0.10 cents. The whole improvement is the fuel price.

2024 to 2025, margin 8.9% to 8.0%. Fuel unit cost declined another 0.33 cents while unit revenue declined 0.46 cents and non-fuel unit cost rose 0.09 cents. Unit revenue declined by more than the fuel price returned. In dollars, revenue rose $2,007m and operating expense $2,389m, with salaries +$969m, other operating +$866m, landing fees +$412m, maintenance +$231m, regional capacity purchase +$177m and special charges +$147m against fuel -$360m and distribution -$122m.

The current run-rate. Trailing twelve months to 30 June 2026 against FY2025: revenue $62,902m, +6.5% and accelerating; operating income $4,873m as reported, +3.4%, against $4,259m excluding special items, down 14.3%; the fuel price $2.98 against $2.44, +22%.▪ The unit figures over the same window are CASM of 17.28 cents against 16.46, +5.0%, and TRASM of 18.73 cents against 17.88, +4.8%, on capacity of 335,759m seat-miles, +1.7% and decelerating. Operating cash flow was $8,913m, +5.7%, and free cash flow $2,544m, tracking. Four of those inflected, and the fuel price is the mechanism in each.

Returns. Return on invested capital peaked at 16.4% in 2016, has not regained that level, and turned down in 2025 to 13.4% from 15.0% as net operating profit after tax declined $180m while average invested capital rose $2,452m. Over the three years to FY2025, $6,112m of additional invested capital produced $1,930m of additional net operating profit, 31.6%. The FY2023 window (289.6%) measures the rebound from the 2020 loss and says nothing about the productivity of new capital.

Cash conversion. Free cash flow was 0.76x net income in 2025 and has exceeded 1.0x in three of the last ten years. Capital expenditure has run near twice depreciation since 2022. Customer prepayments are what make operating cash flow large relative to profit: advance ticket sales and frequent-flyer deferred revenue grew from $8,613m in 2016 to $15,908m in 2025, and that $7,295m of growth is inside operating cash flow.

Leverage through the cycle. Total debt including finance leases peaked at $34,492m at YE2021 and was $24,988m at YE2025. Interest coverage ran 4.8x to 6.5x in 2016-2019, went negative in 2020-2021, bottomed at 1.31x in 2022 and recovered to 3.43x in 2025, still below the pre-2020 band. Interest expense declined from $1,956m in 2023 to $1,373m in 2025.

CASM-ex for 2016-2018 is not published on a consistent basis; the 2019-2022 figures are from the 10-K statistics tables and the 2023-2025 figures from the quarterly earnings releases, so the series changes source mid-way. Mainline and regional fleet counts are disclosed for 2025 only (1,066 and 424), and the mainline/regional passenger revenue split was withdrawn after the FY2018 10-K.

Capacity growth ran 6.8% and 6.1% in 2024-2025 and halved to 3.4% and 3.5% in the first two quarters of 2026, with load factor improving to 83.4%, which points to a supply constraint and a deliberate cut. Unit revenue declined in 2024 and 2025 and turned up 12.5% on PRASM in Q2-2026 behind five fare increases. Unit cost excluding fuel was flat in 2025 at +0.4% and inflected to +5.9% and +6.1% in the first two quarters of 2026, which management attributes to the close-in capacity removal. Fuel efficiency improved 7.3% in six years. Passengers per employee has declined: 181m passengers on 113,200 employees in 2025 against 162m on 95,900 in 2019. Cargo volume is flat over six years and the whole revenue gain is yield. Ancillary fees per passenger rose from $14.77 to $26.51.

Management quotes another set of metrics as growth rates on calls without reconciling them to a reported line, so none of them has a multi-year series: premium-cabin revenue, Basic Economy revenue, contracted business revenue, co-brand new accounts, card spend, net promoter score, on-time departure rate and seat cancellation rate. 14. Expectations: internal, external and base rates

Management and the street agree on 2026, which is guided, and on the direction of 2027. They part on the 2027 level: management's floor is a 10% adjusted pre-tax margin, consensus implies about 9%, and the gap is roughly $2 of adjusted EPS, or about one point of unit revenue.

The internal record. Fifteen quarterly guides since Q4-2022 produced seven results above the range, six inside and two below, both in 2023 and both caused by fuel or a contract accrual inside the quarter. The mean beat against the midpoint is $0.14 across all fifteen and $0.25 excluding Q1-2023. Annual guidance is a different instrument: 2018 and 2019 beat the January range, 2023 and 2024 came in inside it, 2025 finished $0.88 below the floor, and 2026 has been cut twice. Leskinen stated the mechanism directly in April 2025: "we typically build a lot of contingency in the guide. And our $11.50 to $13.50 doesn't really have contingency left. Our quarterly guide still does."

What management has stopped guiding. The quarterly Investor Update gave fourteen guided lines in January 2019, nine in January 2023, four in January 2024, one in October 2024 and three in July 2026. Adjusted pre-tax margin guidance last appeared in January 2023, net leverage in July 2023, capacity as a table row in October 2023, and unit revenue and unit cost in January 2024. Fuel price returned in April 2026 when it became the binding variable. Over the same period the qualitative commitments became firmer: "Our confidence... has never been higher" and "we will absolutely trend below 2 turns."

The external record. United has beaten the pre-print adjusted-EPS consensus for sixteen consecutive quarters, the last miss being Q2-2022. Entering the year, consensus understated United in seven of eight non-pandemic years with a median error of +13.0%; the one overstatement was 2025, and 2026 will be the second, a 23.4% cut already taken. Both overstatements are the two years in which fuel rose sharply into the forecast.

Where the base rate is most uncomfortable for both. Consensus FY2027 revenue growth of 4.8% and an operating margin of 9.8% together imply fuel near $3.50 a gallon. Under management's own retention framing, if fuel goes to $3.50 or below then part of the 2026 fare increase is given back and revenue undershoots $71,183m; if fuel stays above it the margin does. The two consensus lines are mutually consistent only inside a narrow band.▪

United releases after the close and holds its call the next morning, so the next-session move blends both. Every print in this window beat the pre-print adjusted-EPS consensus, with a median beat of 7.9%; the median next-session reaction was -0.6% and the mean +1.2%. Removing the two sessions that followed capital-allocation and fleet decisions takes the mean of the rest to -1.6%.

Quarter Reaction (and five sessions) What the market reacted to
2023:Q3, 18 Oct 2023 (9.7%) / (12.4%) A beat against consensus and a miss against the company's own July guide of $3.85-4.35. Fuel came in $0.30 a gallon above the July midpoint, which the CFO said "more than accounts for the entirety of the reduced outlook"; Tel Aviv service was suspended, about 2% of capacity; Q4 was guided to about $1.80 against a $2.10 pre-print consensus, with unit cost guided up 3.5% and a further 1.5-point risk
2023:Q4, 23 Jan 2024 +5.3% / +9.5% FY2024 guided to $9.00-11.00 with the MAX 9 grounding, 79 aircraft and about 8% of Q1 capacity, fully inside a Q1 loss guide of $(0.85)-$(0.35) against a $(0.20) consensus. The annual guide survived a grounding seventeen days old
2024:Q1, 17 Apr 2024 +17.4% / +30.2% The largest single session of the decade outside 2020. A $(0.15) loss against $(0.57), and a fleet and capital reset: capex cut from about $9bn to $6.5bn, deliveries put at 61 narrowbodies and 5 widebodies against 183 contractual, MAX 10 positions through 2027 converted to MAX 9s, and a stated policy of scheduling about 90% of expected deliveries. FY2024 consensus moved from $9.43 to $10.22 within nine days
2024:Q3, 16 Oct 2024 +12.4% / +16.3% The first buyback authorisation since 2020, $1.5bn funded from free cash flow with net leverage at 2.7x, together with the statement that "the inflection we spoke about on our last call has happened" as unprofitable domestic capacity exited, and a Q4 guide above consensus. The stock added a further 39.2% over the next twenty sessions
2025:Q3, 16 Oct 2025 (5.6%) / (7.5%) The print and the guide both exceeded consensus and FY2025 consensus rose from $10.31 to $10.86 across the print. Inside the release: revenue 0.4% below consensus, a Q3 pre-tax margin the CFO said would have been a point higher without the Newark disruption, and a Q4 range sized for "one act of God, not two" with the federal shutdown in its third week. A market-wide move is the other possible cause
2026:Q1, 22 Apr 2026 (5.6%) / (6.9%) FY2026 guidance cut to $7.00-11.00 from $12.00-14.00 on the fuel shock, using the 17 April forward curve with Q2 at about $4.30 a gallon, Tel Aviv and Dubai flying pulled (1.5 points of capacity) and second-half capacity cut to flat-to-+2% from a schedule sold in at about +4%. Q1 itself beat

In none of these sessions did the quarter's own surprise drive the reaction. Guidance for the next period drove four of the six, including 2025:Q3, where the guide was above consensus and the stock declined; capital-allocation and fleet decisions drove the two largest positive moves. The largest single-session decline after a print in the last ten years is 12.1% on 19 October 2017, after the Q3-2017 call guided Q4 pre-tax margin to 3-5% into a Spirit-led fare war.

What the pricing record shows

The 2024-2025 gain was mostly a multiple. Across the decade adjusted EPS went from $8.65 to $10.62, up 22.8% or 2.3% a year, while the share price went from $72.88 to $111.82, up 53.4%, and the trailing adjusted multiple from 8.4x to 10.5x. Of the $38.94 of price change per share, $16.60 corresponds to the earnings change at the 2016 multiple and $22.34 to the multiple change at 2025 earnings.

The beat streak has not moved the stock. All fifteen prints since Q4-2022 beat consensus by a median of 8.6% and the median next-session reaction was zero. Over the same period both annual ranges that were issued and then cut moved about 23% at the midpoint within six months.

The street's stance and the share price point in opposite directions and the difference is a multiple. Twenty-four buy-equivalent recommendations, two holds and no sells with a mean target 45% above the close, against a twelve-month total return of +0.4%. The mean target is 10.6x the FY2027 consensus the stock already has; the median month-end forward multiple since 2016 is 7.6x and the highest print outside the loss window is 11.3x.

The leverage gap to Delta is 0.25x and the forward-multiple gap is two turns. United's estimate dispersion for FY2027 is 12.5% of the mean across 26 estimates against Delta's 7.4% across 24.

United's price to FY2026E adjusted consensus is 11x and to FY2027E is 7.3x, against Delta at 13x and 9.3x, Southwest at 12x and 8.2x, Alaska at not meaningful and 8.4x, and American at not meaningful and 5.9x. 17. Forward model summary

A driver-based operating model to FY2032, built on the reported H1-2026 actuals for 2026 and forecast from there. Year 0 is FY2025 and every FY2025 line ties to the reported statements. No multiple is applied to any projection and nothing is discounted.

Revenue compounds 5.0% a year from FY2026 to FY2032, capacity supplying 3.0 points and unit revenue 2.0. Operating margin recovers from 5.9% in 2026 to 8.4% by 2028 and then flattens between 9.3% and 9.7%, so the terminal adjusted pre-tax margin of 9.3% is below management's stated 2027 floor and well below the mid-teens aspiration.▪ Free cash flow is the slowest line to recover: cumulative FY2026-FY2032 free cash flow of $20,756m against cumulative adjusted net income of $34,386m is a 60% conversion rate, and FY2027 converts 32% against management's "about 50% for the next few years", because adjusted capital expenditure averages $7,914m a year against depreciation starting at $3,063m. On leverage the model agrees with management: FY2027 adjusted EBITDAR near $9,350m against adjusted net debt reduced by free cash flow less about $620m of repurchases gives roughly 1.9x [estimate: FY2027 EBITDA plus fixed operating lease expense grown from the trailing $975m, with operating lease obligations held flat, which understates the denominator drag from further sale-leasebacks].

The fuel pass-through is modelled as a separate driver because fuel was 21.0% of operating expense in FY2025 and 30.8% in Q2-2026, and a $1.00 move in the price per gallon is $4,663m on FY2025 volumes, 1.1x the entire FY2025 pre-tax income. Most of the 2026 increase is a cost recovery that partly reverses, which a single unit-revenue growth rate would not show. The base case recovers 85% of a fuel increase, which is what Q2-2026 realised on the reported unit figures, and gives back 50% of any relief in FY2027 and 35% thereafter, between the CEO's April and July positions.

The bear produces cumulative negative free cash flow of $7,816m over the seven years through a compounding gap: unit revenue grows 1.9% a year while non-fuel unit cost grows about 3.5% and the fuel line never gives anything back. Profit sharing declines to zero by 2032, which offsets about $1,400m of the decline. That path is what the class base rate describes, since the median margin fade from a peak across the six US carriers is 2.0 points a year and all six faded from the 2015-2016 peak.

The bull reaches a 10.5% adjusted pre-tax margin in 2027, matching management's floor, and 14.2% by 2029, matching the aspiration, with cumulative free cash flow of $47,339m. A 14%-plus pre-tax margin occurred in 10 of 103 US airline-years, all of them in 2015-2018 at jet fuel between $1.25 and $2.03 a gallon against $2.70 in the bull, and United's own maximum pre-tax margin over eighteen years is 11.1%. The bull's FY2027 incremental operating margin of 68% also exceeds United's best clean year, 54.8% in 2019.

Fuel looks smaller than its gross exposure only because the model recovers most of an increase and gives back a third to a half of a decline. With pass-through switched off, a $0.50 move swings FY2027 adjusted EPS by $9.56; with it, by $4.62. The 2026 experience is the first number, because United reprices with a one-to-two-quarter lag and within a year the gross exposure is what shows up. Structural unit revenue dominates the terminal year because 100bp compounds over six years on a revenue base above $80bn; over one year it is worth $2.37. Capital expenditure changes free cash flow dollar for dollar and nothing else, and the street's own FY2027 capex range of $5.0bn to $8.8bn is wider than the FY2027 free-cash-flow consensus of $2,624m.

Assumptions and where each is contested

Two assumptions in this set are contradicted by the company's own record and both flatter the base case. Headcount elasticity to capacity is modelled at 0.55x, while seat-miles per employee declined from 2.97m in 2019 to 2.92m in 2025, which is an elasticity of 1.14x, and the year-over-year readings are 0.65x, 0.57x, 0.90x and 1.60x for the most recent four periods; headcount was 117,500 at 30 June 2026 against 113,200 at YE2025, up 3.80% in six months against capacity up 3.43%. At 1.0x, headcount grows 2.8% a year instead of 1.54% and adds about $2,070m to the FY2032 salary line. Other operating expense is modelled to grow 3.2 points faster than passenger volume, which equals the single most favourable observation on record: the spread was +5.6 points in 2019, +7.0 in 2024, +5.3 in 2025 and +4.2 in H1-2026, and only the one quarter Q2-2026 came in at +3.2. Two extra points compounded over six years on a $10,758m FY2026 base adds about $1,400m to FY2032 expense. Correcting both removes roughly $3.5bn from FY2032 operating income, which would take the terminal operating margin from 9.7% to under 6%.▪

Several other assumptions are weak in the same direction. The FY2027 and terminal fuel prices ($3.30 and $3.05) imply Gulf Coast spot 20% and 27% below the August 2026 level, against a base rate in which the median change in the year after a spike is +1.9%; a terminal price flat in nominal terms while non-fuel unit cost inflates 3% a year lowers real fuel cost through the whole terminal period. Structural unit-revenue growth of 2.2% a year is drawn from the one window (2019-2025) that contains the post-pandemic repricing; the same calculation gives +0.1% a year for 2016-2019 and +1.2% for 2022-2025, so the 1.9% bear is above two of the three measured windows. Landing fees are modelled at 6.0% growth with a bear equal to the base, against a six-year compound rate of 7.15% and +9.3% in H1-2026. Maintenance at 6.5% compares with a six-year rate of 10.66% and +10.3% in H1-2026. Regional capacity purchase at 4.0% compares with +8.2% in H1-2026. Salary growth at 3.4% with a 3.5% bear compares with 3.63% a year realised since 2019, and the pilot agreement becomes amendable on 30 September 2027 with openers planned for early 2027, inside the forecast window, against a CFO estimate that a full ratification round costs 2-3 points of unit cost, about $1.0bn a year. Depreciation at 6.0% is the one driver erring against the company, since the line compounded 4.26% a year since 2019 and grew 4.0% in H1-2026 while sale-leasebacks removed assets as fast as capital expenditure added them. Adjusted capital expenditure of $8.2bn a year for 2027-2029 is above management's own $7-9bn midpoint and 12% above the street, and United has spent below its capex guidance three years running. A 1.5% annual reduction in the share count implies retiring about 30m shares, roughly $3,300m at the current price, against base-case FY2027 free cash flow of $1,128m and a stated priority of reaching investment grade.

The revenue lines agree within about a point in all three years, so the entire difference is the incremental margin on that revenue. Solving the model for the consensus FY2027 EPS of $15.06 requires structural unit-revenue growth of 5.7% instead of 2.2%; solving it for management's 10% floor requires 8.0% and produces $17.75 of adjusted EPS. United's realised unit-revenue growth was 2.6% a year over 2019-2025 and zero over 2022-2025.▪ The base case also takes management's own FY2027 unit-cost guide at its favourable end, +2.0% against the guided +2% to +3%, so the gap to consensus is unit revenue. Against the base rate, the base-case FY2027 adjusted EPS of $10.91 is close to the median outcome of about $10.50 from the 41-observation incremental-margin distribution, and consensus is at about the 80th percentile.

18. Risks

Ranked by probability-weighted pre-tax effect over the next 24 months.

1. Fuel price, without full pass-through (realised). United buys on index-linked contracts and does not hedge. A one-dollar change in the price of a barrel moves 2026 fuel expense by about $116m, so $0.10 a gallon is about $487m a year and about $122m a quarter [estimate: the disclosed per-barrel sensitivity converted at 42 gallons, cross-checked against Q2-2026 consumption of 1,219m gallons]. Full-year 2026 fuel is "almost $6 billion higher" than the plan at the start of the year. The Q3 guide assumes $3.69 a gallon; the global average jet price reached $171.01 a barrel in the first week of September, about $4.07 a gallon before taxes and into-plane cost, which is roughly $700m for a full quarter at that level [estimate: 1.2bn gallons at the gap to the assumption]. Leading indicators: Gulf Coast jet spot and the crack spread, the Strait of Hormuz, the forward curve on each Investor Update date, and booked yields.

2. Yield give-back when fuel recedes and capacity returns. Each point of yield is about $580m of 2026 passenger revenue [estimate: FY2025 passenger revenue grown to the consensus 2026 base], and a five-point give-back is about $2.9bn of revenue at close to full flow-through. The consensus FY2027 step-up of $5.19 a share is the exposure in per-share terms: it assumes yields hold while fuel normalises. Kirby has conceded that 10% of the Q2 increase was capacity-driven and that United's own Q4 domestic schedule "will be adjusted downward when finalized". If fuel instead stays near $4, demand elasticity is the other side: management modelled it and 23% of Q2 and 8% of Q3 were sold at pre-spike prices. Leading indicators: published 2027 industry schedules, Boeing's delivery rate, United's own aircraft count, and airfare CPI. Working against the risk: 80 aircraft retirements planned for 2027 and FAA caps that hold hub capacity flat for every carrier.

3. Aircraft and engine delivery slippage. The fleet plan depends on 581 firm orders at 30 June 2026, of which expected deliveries for the last six months of 2026 were 63 against 121 contractual. Purchase commitments are $57.0bn with $12.6bn contractual in 2026 against about $7.5bn of expected spend. Slippage keeps older aircraft flying, which raises maintenance and defers the 2-3 point unit-cost benefit of gauge; the 80 planned 2027 retirements depend on arrivals. The grounding precedent is sized: the January 2024 door-plug directive grounded all 79 of United's MAX 9s and cost more than $200m in one quarter, and the quarter produced a $79m pre-tax loss. Leading indicators: Boeing's monthly deliveries and the MAX 10 type certificate, GE and Pratt engine availability, the expected-against-contractual table in each 10-Q, and any disposition of the A350 order.

4. Hub capacity caps, air traffic control and government funding. Hourly caps at Newark and O'Hare were each extended for a further year and an FAA approach change lowered San Francisco landing rates; the November 2025 shutdown forced cuts at about 40 airports and cost about $250m pre-tax. The 2026-Q2 10-Q now lists "Regulatory or Court Decisions Restricting Our Capacity Targets" as a key trend. The 2025 precedent sizes a hub event at about a point of quarterly margin, roughly $150m [estimate: a point on about $15bn of quarterly revenue]. Leading indicators: FAA order expiry dates, controller staffing, the federal fiscal year ending 30 September 2026, and DOT on-time and cancellation statistics for Newark.

5. MileagePlus and the Chase relationship. About $3.2bn of partner revenue is recognised annually and $7,971m of deferred revenue was outstanding at 30 June 2026. A 10% reduction in partner revenue is about $320m a year of high-margin revenue [estimate]. The Credit Card Competition Act would require dual-network routing for large issuers, and the DOT inquiry into the four largest loyalty programs has been open since September 2024 without an announced outcome; the FY2025 10-K added program changes "as a result of legal or regulatory requirements" to the loyalty risk factor. The contract is in its sunset phase with renegotiation not started. Leading indicators: the legislative calendar, the DOT outcome, and co-brand new accounts and card spend each quarter.

6. Labour cost and work actions. 83% of 113,200 employees are unionised. The flight-attendant agreement was ratified in May 2026 after members rejected the July 2025 tentative agreement, leaving a $742m ratification-payment liability at 30 June 2026. The pilot agreement becomes amendable on 30 September 2027 with openers planned for early 2027. Management's own estimate is that a full ratification round adds 2-3 points of unit cost, about $1.0bn a year [estimate: 2.5% of FY2025 CASM-ex on FY2025 capacity]. Salaries rose 7.9% in H1-2026. Leading indicators: mediation filings, the ALPA opener, and peer pay scales.

7. Competitive response at the hubs. American grew at O'Hare through 2025 and 2026; on Kirby's own figures United's O'Hare profit was about $100m lower in 2025 than it would have been without that growth. Delta's unit revenue remains 9% above United's on an airline-only basis. Leading indicators: American's O'Hare schedule filings and the quarterly DOT origin-destination share data management cites.

8. Leverage, covenants and ratings. Total debt including finance leases and other financial liabilities was $26.5bn at 30 June 2026, $33.7bn with operating leases, and $928m falls due in the second half of 2026. Covenants require $2.0bn of minimum liquidity and 1.6-to-1.0 collateral coverage, both met with wide headroom. What has moved is the denominator: trailing adjusted EBITDAR declined 10.5% in a year on fuel, and the investment-grade objective needs H2-2026 adjusted EBITDAR up 14.4% year over year. Leading indicators: agency actions, liquidity, capital spending, and the 4 December 2026 expiry of the tax-benefits preservation plan.

9. Geopolitical airspace closures and international demand. Tel Aviv and Dubai service was suspended during the 2026 conflict and Russian overflight has been suspended since 2022. International is 41% of total operating revenue. The direct route revenue is small; the exposure runs through fuel and through Middle East carrier capacity when it returns.

10. Safety events, groundings and IT outages. Precedents at United: 79 MAX 9s grounded in January 2024 (more than $200m), more than 50 Pratt-powered 777s grounded in February 2021, and the July 2024 CrowdStrike outage (about a point of quarterly capacity). The FY2025 10-K discloses that United's "use of AI applications has resulted in certain immaterial cybersecurity incidents".

11. The demand cycle. The April 2025 recession scenario guided $7-9 of EPS on 5 points less revenue, which is the company's own sizing of a downturn. Contracted business revenue grew 27% and premium 16% in Q2-2026, so current bookings show no demand destruction. Leading indicators: the air traffic liability trend, TSA throughput, corporate booking growth and Basic Economy volume.

12. Regulatory, environmental and tariff costs. Tariffs on aircraft, engines and parts including retaliation; CORSIA offsets expected by January 2028; sustainable-fuel premiums; PFAS designation; a certified vaccination-mandate class action. None is sized in the filings.

How they correlate. The two quarters of 2026 are the template: a fuel spike, airspace closures, capacity removal, a halted buyback, a defensive $3.7bn raise and cap extensions at two hubs, arriving together and moving the annual guide by $4 a share at the midpoint. The forward bad quarter is fuel above $4 while a competitor adds capacity at a capped hub, the MAX 10 slips again so the 2027 retirements are deferred and maintenance rises, pilots open negotiations, and a federal funding lapse cuts schedules. Each has a disclosed precedent inside the last 24 months. Two risks offset: a fuel spike removes marginal competitor capacity, which helps pricing while hurting cost, and delivery delays cut capital spending and lift free cash flow while raising unit cost.

19. Source disclosure

Company documents. Sixteen annual reports on Form 10-K, FY2010 through FY2025; the FY2016-FY2025 filings supply the ten-year series and the FY2010-FY2015 filings the Continental merger accounting and integration charges; six quarterly reports on Form 10-Q through the quarter ended 30 June 2026; the quarterly earnings releases and Investor Updates filed as exhibits to Form 8-K from January 2019 to 15 July 2026, which is where United publishes guidance and its non-GAAP reconciliations; nine proxy statements on Schedule 14A, 2018 through 2026; and SEC XBRL company facts for the ten-year income statement, balance sheet, cash flow, share count and repurchase series.

Transcripts. Forty earnings calls, Q3-2016 through Q2-2026, contiguous; forty-four investor-conference and investor-day transcripts covering every year from 2016 to 2026, including the November 2016 Investor Day and the June 2021 United Next event.

Investor presentations. Five decks, of which two were analysed in depth: the June 2021 United Next investor event (47 slides) and the January 2023 Q4-2022 earnings presentation (14 slides). The November 2016 Investor Day (104 slides, no text layer), the June 2020 MileagePlus investor presentation (47 slides) and a March 2022 conference deck were not analysed slide by slide; the MileagePlus presentation was read from a parsed text extract, and it supplies the loyalty-program anchor used in Sections 1 and 4.

Peer and value-chain filings. FY2019 and FY2025 annual reports and 2026 quarterly reports for Delta, American, Southwest, Alaska and JetBlue; FY2025 annual reports for Boeing, GE Aerospace, RTX, Howmet, TransDigm, SkyWest, Republic Airways, Expeditors and Expedia; Boeing's Q2-2026 quarterly report.

Market and consensus data. Bloomberg terminal, live throughout and pulled 11 September 2026: daily prices and total returns from January 2014 (3,192 sessions), monthly forward consensus and forward multiples from January 2014, dated fiscal-year consensus snapshots for FY2015-FY2028, quarterly pre-print consensus and announcement dates from 2011, annual fundamentals from FY2013, per-analyst recommendations and targets (30 rows), consensus dispersion by fiscal year and quarter, peer consensus and leverage, two cash bonds with yields and ratings, and the 39-row comparable-company table.

Series built from those sources. A reconciled ten-year annual series and a twelve-quarter series from the filings, cross-checked against XBRL, a third-party workbook and Bloomberg; a US-carrier capacity and traffic series for 2014-2025 from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics via FRED; a 103-observation panel of US airline-years for the margin, growth and fuel base rates; a peer financial series computed on one definition from each carrier's own XBRL facts; a guidance scorecard rebuilt from the Investor Updates and earnings releases; and the four price and multiple charts in Section 15.

Gaps and failures. No sell-side research covering United appears in the subscribed report set: zero hits across 376 reports, so the external view is built from Bloomberg consensus and recommendation data, the analysts' own questions on the calls, and dated press summaries. Broker note text is paywalled. No rating-agency reports are available in any subscribed store, so the corporate family ratings behind the issue ratings quoted in Section 12 are not confirmed. Proxy-adviser recommendations on the 2025 and 2026 say-on-pay votes are not available. The textual year-over-year diff of Items 1 and 7 could not be run; the risk-factor diffs in Section 18 were built directly from the ten archived filings. The FY2010-FY2015 filings are used only for the merger accounting, so the Continental integration years are not reconstructed as a revenue and margin path. The June 2020 MileagePlus presentation is hosted on a page that times out, and a parsed text extract was used.

Discrepancies between sources, and what was used.

  • FY2016 and FY2017 exist on two revenue bases in the filing record. The recast figures from the FY2018 10-K are used ($36,558m and $37,784m), which differ from the as-filed figures by $2m and $48m; Bloomberg's series uses the as-filed basis for FY2016 and the recast basis from FY2018, so any Bloomberg comparison crossing 2017/2018 mixes them.
  • FY2017 and FY2018 operating income differs between the FY2018 and FY2019 filings by $53m and $63m because of the lease standard, with net income unchanged. The later presentation is used, and the same change moves FY2017-FY2018 capital expenditure and operating cash flow.
  • Bloomberg's EBITDA field for United adds operating lease cost net of sublease income ($861m in 2025, $820m in 2024, $886m in 2023, each tying to the lease note), so it is an EBITDAR. Leverage computed on that field is roughly half a turn lower than on an EBITDA basis.
  • Bloomberg's total debt includes operating lease liabilities and excludes the other financial liabilities inside the reported debt captions; net debt for FY2016-FY2018 differs from the balance-sheet computation by a constant $71-75m, unreconciled and immaterial.
  • The FY2025 passenger revenue summed from the four quarterly releases is $53,437m against $53,438m in the annual report, and the four quarters of revenue sum to $59,071m against $59,070m. The annual figures are used.
  • FY2017 adjusted EPS is $6.76 on Bloomberg and $6.85 in the company's own release; the company figure is used, which moves the FY2017 trailing multiple from 10.0x to 9.8x.
  • Recommendation counts and target prices differ by vendor: 26 recommendations and a $159.19 mean on Bloomberg, 18 and $155.91 on MarketBeat, 25 and $159.20 on StockAnalysis. The Bloomberg panel is used.
  • Adjusted EBITDAR was redefined on 1 January 2025, which raised the FY2024 figure by $662m and moved reported net leverage for that date from 2.43x to 2.25x. Both published figures appear in Section 12 with the date attached.

Unreconciled figures inside this document.

  • Enterprise value is $52,684m on the cover and in Section 16, $1,765m below the $35,653m of market capitalisation plus the $18,796m of net debt printed beside it; that enterprise value implies net debt of $17,031m at the same date. Every EV multiple in the front matter and in Sections 15 and 16 is computed on $52,684m.
  • Bloomberg's gross and net leverage fields in Section 12 do not reconcile with each other. Gross debt to trailing EBITDA of 4.28x on $31.0bn of debt implies EBITDA of $7,251m; net debt to trailing EBITDA of 2.16x on $18.8bn implies $8,702m. Both are printed as published.
  • Adjusted EBITDAR for FY2025 is $8,513m in Section 13.1 and $8,969m in Section 12, and for FY2024 $8,844m and $9,066m. The Section 13.1 row adds total operating lease cost to EBITDA; Section 12 uses the figure behind United's own reported net leverage, and every leverage statement elsewhere is on the Section 12 basis.
  • Cash from third-party mile sales is estimated at $5.8-6.4bn in Section 1 and total partner cash at $5,100-5,700m in Section 5, by two methods whose ranges do not overlap. Sections 7, 8 and 17 use the Section 5 range.
  • United's FY2025 earnings per share in Section 16 are $10.44 adjusted and $10.12 GAAP, against $10.62 and $10.20 in Section 13.1. The comparable table is on the vendor's definitions for all thirty-nine rows and Section 13 is on the company's.
  • Return on invested capital for FY2025 is 13.4% on the effective-rate series in Section 3 and 12.6% on the statutory-rate, lease-adjusted series used against peers. The ten-year averages on the two bases are 8.3% and 7.9%, and the 7.9% figure is the one quoted in Sections 3 and 8.
  • The print statistics in Section 15 run on two samples. The twelve quarters in the table give a median beat of 7.9% and a median next-session move of -0.6%; the fifteen prints since Q4-2022 are quoted at a median beat of 8.6% and a median move of zero, and the three earliest of those prints are not shown.
  • The third-quarter fuel gap in Section 18 is given as roughly $700m. The September price of $4.07 a gallon against the $3.69 guidance basis is $0.38 on about 1.2bn gallons, or about $460m; the $4.07 excludes taxes and into-plane cost, which are not disclosed.
  • United Next is 270 aircraft ordered in Section 9 and 186 MAX plus 70 A321neos newly ordered in the Appendix A delivery-schedule caption.

Web sources. Twenty-six pages across twenty domains are cited for material claims, each with its access date inline and its relevant passage quoted in Appendix B: iata.org (three pages), oag.com (three), transtats.bts.gov (two), cnbc.com (two), and one each from aviationweek.com, alpa.org, boeing.com, cirium.com, jdpower.com, npr.org, starlink.com, stratechery.com, thepointsguy.com, travelmarketreport.com, sherwood.news, airwaysmag.com, news.jetblue.com, nextbigfuture.com, theflightbrief.com and ir.united.com.

Claims marked [web, unverified]. One, for the reader to spot-check: the US-China weekly frequency schedule rising from 50 to 100 by December 2026, which is trade-press reporting of a bilateral arrangement the carriers do not publish. One further figure, the 600-800 millisecond latency of geostationary aviation Wi-Fi, comes from a secondary technical source and is tagged [web, secondary].

Estimates. Thirty-six figures above are tagged [estimate:] with their method and bounds. By method: eight apply a disclosed company sensitivity or formula to current volumes (fuel per barrel and per gallon, the interest-rate sensitivities, the profit-sharing tiers, the per-point value of unit revenue and of a labour round); eight are ratio arithmetic on two disclosed figures (the per-share pay weight, the buyback value transfer, two stake market values, the merger's revenue multiple, the minority contribution to a partner, a hub event as a share of quarterly revenue); seven rebuild a disclosed table forward or backward (the debt stack at 30 June 2026, regional capacity weights, unit cost excluding fuel, regional seat-miles and regional unit cost, two EBITDAR bridges); three scale a disclosed historical anchor to current volumes (third-party mile cash, the loyalty program's share of profit, pro-forma peer capacity); two solve management's disclosed growth rates against a reported revenue base (premium-cabin revenue, loyalty revenue); one builds a market pool bottom-up (the US domestic passenger pool, bracketed two ways); one is a cost of capital on the capital asset pricing model; and the remainder are single-step conversions stated inline. Every estimate is reported as a range where the inputs support only a range.

One correction. Say-on-pay support of 86.3% in 2025 is the second-lowest result in United's record; the 2021 annual meeting recorded 82%, which is printed in the 2022 proxy's five-year table.

20. What we still don't know, and what would resolve it

Five gaps are large enough to change a conclusion.

  1. What the flying business earns once MileagePlus is removed. The program's cash and margin can only be estimated, and on that estimate the transport operation is left near an 11% EBITDA margin before depreciation and interest. If that is right, the competitive-advantage assessment in Section 3 is partly an assessment of a contract that expires in 2029. Resolved by: segment disclosure, which the CFO said in mid-2025 he was working to provide "at some point next year" and which the Q2-2026 quarterly report does not contain.
  2. What Chase pays per mile, and how many miles are issued and redeemed. Aggregate third-party mile cash is estimable at $5,100-5,700m; price and volume separately are not, so neither the renewal arithmetic nor the "double the EBITDA" claim can be tested. Resolved by: a disclosed cash figure of the kind Delta and American publish, or the terms of a renewed agreement.
  3. Whether regional flying earns its capital. United Express is 424 aircraft, about 6.1% of capacity, a $2,693m capacity-purchase fee plus the fuel and landing fees United pays directly, and $18.9bn of future commitments. The mainline and regional passenger revenue split was withdrawn after the FY2018 filing, so the unit is not measurable from the accounts. Whether it loses money at the margin decides whether the gauge plan is growth or margin repair. Resolved by: DOT Form 41 segment data, or a restored mainline/regional split.
  4. What the Pacific position is worth if the two policy facts reverse. Pacific unit revenue is 27% above 2019 on capacity 6% above, and it is held there by US-China frequency caps and the closure of Russian airspace. A return of Pacific unit revenue to the domestic index would remove roughly $700-800m of revenue at close to full incremental margin. Resolved by: the allocation of the frequencies rising to 100 a week by December 2026, and the Pacific unit-revenue print as they are used.
  5. Whether United's operational reliability leads. The brand premium in Section 3 depends on it, and United's supporting measure is an internal net promoter score whose level is never published; the two independent measures available place United fourth in North America on arrival punctuality and outside the top three in all three cabin segments on customer satisfaction. Resolved by: the DOT on-time and completion series, carrier by carrier, on a full-year basis.

Further open questions, by where they bite.

  • Ancillary fees, $4,800m and 9.0% of passenger revenue, are disclosed only as an annual total. No split by bag, seat, change or preferred seating exists, so a line that produced about a quarter of the per-passenger revenue gain since 2019 has no driver and no peer comparison.
  • Premium revenue is not disclosed and the two management sources for Q4-2025 growth disagree; the seat count (27.4m, 12.3% of seats flown) and the revenue metric describe different populations and are not reconciled.
  • Hub-level economics. Management says it computes hub and route margins to within a point. None is disclosed, so the capacity caps at Newark and O'Hare appear in the risk inventory without a quantified effect on contribution.
  • Contracted business revenue is quoted as a growth rate every quarter and never as a level, so the corporate share of passenger revenue is unconstrained.
  • Kinective Media revenue has never been disclosed, and management's target to double it in 2025 and again in 2026 cannot be scored.
  • Sale-leaseback capacity. Gains were $427m in 2025 and $796m in the first half of 2026, inside operating income. Proceeds, aircraft counts and implied lease rates are undisclosed, so whether the gains recur in 2027, and therefore whether reported 2026 margins repeat, is unknown.
  • The cash-tax path. $10.6bn of federal loss carryforwards remain and the 4.9%-trigger preservation plan expires on 4 December 2026. Whether it is renewed, and how fast the carryforwards are consumed, is the largest single swing in the free-cash-flow conversion management guides to.
  • Contracted labour cost and amendable dates. Salaries rose 46% on 15.9% more capacity between 2019 and 2025. The scheduled increases already inside the signed ALPA, AFA, IAM and IBT agreements are not set out anywhere, so the 2-3% unit-cost path for 2027 has no contractual floor under it.
  • What happens to unit cost if the MAX 10 slips again while the 80 planned 2027 retirements still land. No scenario prices holding those aircraft a further year with their maintenance cost and the foregone gauge benefit.
  • The fuel assumption inside consensus. The brokers' input is not observable, so the FY2027 consensus cannot be restated on a common fuel basis; a $0.50 error moves FY2027 operating income by about $2.4bn before any pass-through.
  • What moved the share price on 16 October 2025. The print beat, the Q4 guide exceeded consensus and the full-year consensus rose across the print, and the stock declined 5.6%. A market-wide move is the other possible cause.
  • No company disclosure exists after 15 July 2026. Nine weeks of the third quarter had elapsed by 11 September 2026 with the jet price above the guidance basis, and the CFO was scheduled to speak at a conference on 16 September 2026.

Appendix A — Investor-presentation insights and key slides

Five United decks are archived for the last decade and the company has held no investor day since June 2021, so the most recent investor-day deck is five years old. The 2021 United Next event and the January 2023 earnings deck give hub-level and aircraft-level economics and the full financial target table the 2021 plan was sold on; the November 2016 Investor Day, the June 2020 MileagePlus financing presentation and the March 2022 J.P. Morgan conference deck are read below them, and the loyalty program's standalone accounts appear in no other document.

  • Hub and regional profitability. United's internal flight-profitability system put its FY2019 long-haul margin about 16 points ahead of American and Delta on the Pacific, 9 points ahead on the Atlantic, level on Deep South America and 8 points ahead overall; the same system put its mid-continent hubs about 10 points behind rival mid-continent hubs while its international gateways ran about 7 points ahead [deck: United Next 2021-06-29, slides 5 and 11]. That is why United's ranking is highest in the markets with the least domestic overlap.
  • The 2018 hub diagnosis in three measures. Departures per spoke 2.8 against 3.6-3.7 at Delta and American, destinations 148 against 165-167, and connecting itineraries 16.8 thousand against 27.5-34.0 thousand [slide 7]. That gap is what the order was placed to close, and it is why the advantage is local and hub-level.
  • Aircraft-level unit economics. An A321neo seats about 55% more than an A319 for about 13% more cost per departure, giving about 27% lower unit cost; incremental MAX 10 unit cost was put 48% below average domestic unit cost, "below 6 cents"; fuel cost per seat on a 700-mile stage was $36 on a 50-seat regional jet, $25 on an A319 and $16 on a MAX 9 [slides 30, 31, 32]. These are the numbers behind the gauge argument in Sections 1, 2 and 17.
  • The cost bridge that failed. 10.21 cents in 2019, plus 0.8 of inflation to 2023, less 0.7 from the $2bn structural cost program and 0.5 from gauge, then plus 0.6 of inflation, less 1.5 from gauge and plus 0.4 from stage length, to about 9.4 cents in 2026 [slide 33]. The plan allowed 1.4 cents of cumulative non-fuel unit-cost inflation across seven years, about 1.9% a year, and it assigned 2.0 of the 2.8 cents of offsets to gauge and asset utilisation. Realised 2025 unit cost excluding fuel was 12.64 cents.
  • The fuel assumption. The 2026 target table assumed $2.20 a gallon [slide 42]. United paid $4.19 in Q2-2026. At that price on 2025 volumes the fuel bill runs roughly $9bn above what the 14% margin target assumed, about 15 points of revenue. When an analyst asked for the macro inputs at the event, the answer was that the prices were in the appendix.
  • The revenue mix that let the plan assume flat unit revenue. The domestic economy cabin excluding Economy Plus produced only 30% of 2019 revenue, planned to decline to 27% by 2026 [slide 25]. This is the closest thing United has published to a cabin-level revenue split, and it bears directly on the premium estimate in Section 1.
  • Premium density against foreign carriers. United's own chart puts it at 44 lie-flat seats per long-haul departure against 32 at American and Delta but 63 at the foreign-flag carriers serving the same hubs [slide 20]. The premium-seat lead is over US rivals, which qualifies the international part of Section 3.
  • The cost-convergence chart behind the current thesis. FY2022 unit cost excluding fuel against 2019: Frontier 29%, Spirit 22%, Southwest 20%, Alaska 19%, Delta 18%, United 15%, JetBlue 14%, American 12% [deck: Q4 2022 earnings presentation 2023-01-18, slide 9]. It measures the rate of change and not the level, which is why Section 8 separates the two.
  • The demand model. Industry domestic revenue as a share of US GDP was 0.71% in 1990-2000, 0.54% in 2001-2010, 0.49% in 2011-2019 and 0.45% in 2022, with management's baseline assuming a return to about 0.49% and stating that "every basis point of improvement is ~1 point of margin" [2023 deck, slides 4 and 9]. United has not updated the series since.
  • Operating reliability as a competitive claim. Flight cancellations from 21 to 31 December 2022: Southwest 39%, Alaska 16%, Spirit 12%, Frontier 10%, Delta 7%, United 5%, JetBlue 4%, American 3%, at broadly similar weather exposure [2023 deck, slide 6]. United attributes its result to technology investment, 5-10% staffing buffers, spare aircraft and lower aircraft utilisation.

  • Widebody capacity through the pandemic. United's widebody fleet was 12% larger at the end of 2022 than at the end of 2019 while American and Delta cut 9% and the leading global carriers 5%; United then flew 36% more Atlantic capacity in July 2023 than in July 2019 against 1% for the industry [2023 deck, slide 7]. That decision is the origin of the Atlantic and Pacific position in Section 4.

  • What the loyalty program earns, on its own accounts. The June-2020 financing presentation is the only document in which United publishes MileagePlus Holdings as a standalone entity. Program EBITDA ran $1,235m (2014), $1,443m (2015), $1,825m (2016), $1,724m (2017), $1,880m (2018), $1,828m (2019) and $1,882m for the twelve months to March 2020, or 25%, 18%, 24%, 27%, 30%, 26% and 33% of United's adjusted EBITDAR [deck: MileagePlus presentation 2020-06-15, slides 22 and 46]. It was produced on $110m of operating expense excluding depreciation, 2.1% of the $5,330m of mile-sale cash, and $6m of depreciation [slide 26]. Every real cost of an award, the seat and the aircraft and the crew, is borne by the airline, so the program's margin and the airline's are not additive.

  • A mile is sold at two prices, bought back at one, and provisioned at sixty-four cents in the dollar. A partner buys 15,000 miles at $0.02 a mile for $300, and the program buys the award seat from United at $0.01 a mile for $150, which the deck labels "a 50% profit". Miles earned by flying work differently: United buys them from the program "at a minimum rate of $0.01 per mile + an additional margin" and the program buys the seat back at $0.01, "(at cost)" [slide 11]. Third-party sales were 71% of mile-sale cash and United 29%, so on the smaller share there is no redemption spread at all. At the illustrative earn rate of 1.5 miles per dollar of partner spend, the program collects about 3.0% of cardholder spend [estimate: $300 of mile revenue on $10,000 of partner spend, from the illustrative transaction on slide 11]. Across the whole $5,330m of 2019 collections, about 2 cents in the dollar went to program operating expense, about 34 cents to EBITDA and about 64 cents to the provision for future redemption [estimate: collections less EBITDA less operating expense; the collections figure is cash and the net-revenue figure accrual] [slide 26].
  • The contract terms the financing forced into public view. United buys miles at a price "subject to adjustment such that MPH's United related EBITDA margin... is at least 20%", a floor that resets by price; the operating agreement between United and the program runs 20 years from closing, so to 2040; the "Chase / Visa co-brand agreements recently extended into 2029", with 3-to-5-year terms for other partners; and award pricing, including a dynamic engine with "more than a dozen pricing triggers" and levers for day of travel, revenue-fare displacement and member status, is set at the program's discretion [slides 12 and 23]. The MileagePlus intellectual property, including member data, the domain names, the Premier and MileagePlus marks and the program software, was moved into a bankruptcy-remote Cayman vehicle that licenses it back for a monthly fee "equal to all revenues of MPH during the previous month", and both United and the program covenanted not to run any other loyalty scheme unless it too was pledged [slides 34 and 36]. On termination, liquidated damages equal the present value of a fixed $1.4bn annual sublicense fee running 30 years, discounted at 10%, less the recovery value of the intellectual property [slide 37]: about $13.2bn gross [estimate: $1.4bn x the 30-year 10% annuity factor of 9.4269] against $6.8bn of debt issued, on an assumed fee 92% the size of what United actually paid the program for miles in 2019. United's FY2025 10-K describes partner terms as "approximately one to five years" and does not repeat the margin floor.
  • Miles are issued faster than they are burned, in every year of the only series United has published. The ratio of miles issued to miles redeemed ran 129%, 125%, 119%, 118%, 122% and 123% from 2014 to 2019, and 140% in the twelve months to March 2020 as redemptions collapsed [slide 22]. Miles issued grew an average 6% a year over 2017-2019 against 4% for miles redeemed, while the program's deferred revenue rose 10.6%, so most of the excess issuance was recognised in the period rather than held on the balance sheet [slides 25 and 26]. Redemptions were 97% travel, and United took 80% of the travel share, so about 78% of redemption volume landed back on United metal [slides 10 and 25].
  • The program generated more cash as the airline stopped flying. In April and May 2020 combined, mile-sale collections halved to about $455m, but miles returned from cancelled flights rose about 126% and exceeded miles redeemed by nearly 3x, so redemption cost turned negative at about ($165m) and net cash flow rose about 80%, to roughly $590m from roughly $330m a year earlier [slide 27]. The deck offers the 2008-09 analogue alongside it: United revenue down 19%, program revenue down 2% [slide 21]. The full year confirmed the shape, with total revenue down 64.5% in 2020 and other operating revenue, which holds the recognised partner-mileage revenue, down 22.5%.
  • The financing priced 36% larger than it was marketed, and the collateral was everything the 2016 plan had counted as unencumbered. The deck syndicated a $5.0bn term loan with a daily cash sweep, a three-month interest reserve, a $2bn parent liquidity covenant and a peak debt-service-coverage ladder rising from 0.75x to 2.00x by 2022 [slides 6, 30, 31 and 32]. United issued $6.8bn on 2 July 2020, $3.8bn of 6.50% notes due 2027 plus a $3.0bn term loan at LIBOR plus 5.25%, near $435m of annual interest against $1,828m of 2019 program EBITDA. The term loan was prepaid in July 2024 and the notes redeemed on 7 July 2025, two years before maturity. Four years earlier the 2016 Investor Day had projected unencumbered assets rising to about $13bn by 2020, made up of aircraft, spare parts, spare engines and routes [deck: 2016 Investor Day 2016-11-15, slide 88]; by mid-2020 each of those, plus the loyalty program, had been pledged or earmarked for the CARES loan.
  • The 2016 plan was $4.8bn of pre-tax earnings initiatives against 2015, and the aggregate never moved. The full table runs network $600m, re-fleeting and upgauge $1,000m, segmentation $1,000m, MileagePlus $300m, revenue management $900m, operational integrity $300m and cost efficiency $700m by 2020, with a column stating how much of each line was unavailable to Delta: network and MileagePlus ~100%, revenue management ~75%, re-fleeting and cost ~50%, segmentation ~25% [slide 96]. Pre-tax income was $4,219m in 2015 and $3,773m, $3,023m, $2,648m and $3,914m in the four years that followed, so 2019 came in $305m below the base year against a $4.0bn plan increment. Fuel cost $1,431m more in 2019 than 2015 and the 2016 labour agreements added 4 points to Q1-2017 unit cost, which accounts for part of it. Segmentation was last quantified on the Q2-2017 call and revenue management on the Q4-2017 call, where Kirby put the realised gain at "our 1.2 points that we're already seeing".
  • The gap to Delta closed, and Delta closed it. The plan's central exhibit is a waterfall from a 2016 operating-margin gap to Delta of (5.6) points to a United premium of about 1.5 points by 2020, a 7.1-point swing in four years [slide 97]. The gap as reported was (5.8) points in 2016, (4.1) in 2019 and (1.2) in 2025. United's own operating margin declined 3.9 points over that span, from 11.9% to 8.0%, while Delta's declined 8.5 points, from 17.6% to 9.2%, so the whole of the 4.6-point convergence came from the peer. United has not finished a year ahead of Delta on operating margin since the plan was published.
  • United hit its 2016 unit-cost target by growing capacity at three times the assumed rate. Slide 77 projected non-fuel unit cost up 3.5-4.5% in 2017 and then "less than 1.0%" a year on average through 2020, stating the projection assumed 1.5% annual capacity growth. Non-fuel unit cost, taken as reported CASM less fuel cost per seat mile, ran about 10.4 cents in 2016 and 2017 and about 10.5 cents in 2018 and 2019, growth of roughly 0.7% a year. Capacity grew 3.5%, 4.9% and 3.5%, so non-fuel cost in dollars rose about 4.3% a year against the roughly 2.5% the plan's own assumptions imply. The departure is datable: slide 9 planned 2017 capacity up 1-2%, and by the Q1-2017 call the guide was "up 2.5% to 3.5%... consistent with our updated guidance from March 15", four months after the event.
  • March 2022 is the last date United presented the 2026 cost target as live. The J.P. Morgan conference deck restates the full United Next fleet case unchanged — 104 seats per short-haul North America departure going to about 134 by 2026, premium seats per departure from 31 to 53, and "Efficient growth will enable 2026 CASM-ex ~(8%) below 2019" [deck: J.P. Morgan Industrials Conference 2022-03-15, slide 8]. Two pages later the same deck guides 2022 capacity down high single digits against 2019, first-quarter unit cost excluding fuel about 18% above 2019, and fuel at $2.99 a gallon on the 4 March forward curve, against the $2.20 the 2026 target table assumed [slide 10]. Reaching the plan's 2023 line from there needed capacity up roughly 27-33% in one year and a 22-point unit-cost reversal. The January 2023 deck dropped the 2019-based targets.

Appendix C — External data sources

One external dataset is available for a company of this type. No figure from it appears anywhere above.

Google Trends search interest. A weekly index of relative search volume for a brand or product, normalised to its own peak within the requested window and geography. For United it would give a demand-side series independent of the company's own bookings: the trend in searches for "United Airlines" against "Delta", "American Airlines" and "Southwest" tests whether the brand-preference shift management describes — hub local share up 7 points since 2019, a 22-point lead among Chicago-based customers — shows up in third-party behaviour, and the same series split by metropolitan area would test it hub by hub. Searches for fare-related terms would also give a weekly measure of demand elasticity through the 2026 fare increases, which is the open question behind yield retention in Sections 6, 8 and 17. It would strengthen Section 4's share discussion and Section 6's demand work. There is no clean free interface, so the series would have to be collected page by page and any pull would be partial.
